💡 Key Takeaways
  • The first Starship upper stage that SpaceX ever successfully recovered won't fly again.
  • According to recent reports, that vehicle, known as Ship 42, launched Nov.
  • Ship 42 made it through Flight 15 in good condition, according to SpaceX founder and CEO Elon Musk, who noted it "could probably be reflown with a few weeks of refurbishment." But that's not going to happen.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The first Starship upper stage that SpaceX ever successfully recovered won't fly again.

According to recent reports, that vehicle, known as Ship 42, launched Nov. 13 on Starship's 15th test flight. A day later, it returned from orbit, nestling softly into the "chopstick" arms of its launch tower at SpaceX's Starbase site in South Texas.

Ship 42 made it through Flight 15 in good condition, according to SpaceX founder and CEO Elon Musk, who noted it "could probably be reflown with a few weeks of refurbishment." But that's not going to happen.

According to recent reports, "In this case, because it's kind of an historic ship, we're going to, I think, not take any chances with the ship and just kind of leave it for public display, because what it's done is historic," Musk remarked on Wednesday (Nov. 18) during a discussion at the TomorrowX Summit.

It has been revealed that he didn't say where Ship would be put on display, but the likeliest locale is Starbase, SpaceX's Starship manufacturing and launch hub. (SpaceX intends to shift most Starship launches to its latest Starbase Louisiana site, but construction has yet to begin on that $100 billion complex.).

Industry observers note that musk participated virtually in the TomorrowX conversation, which was moderated by two friends of his, the venture capitalists Gavin Baker and Antonio Gracias. (TomorrowX took place in Austin, Texas, but Musk was in China on Wednesday as part of President Trump's delegation for his meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping.).

The world's richest man expounded on Ship 42's historic achievement, explaining that it gets SpaceX much closer to the "holy grail of rocketry" — a fully and rapidly reusable launch vehicle.

In a recent development, before Flight 15, SpaceX had already caught Starship's first-stage booster, known as Super Heavy, on three separate occasions, and it had reflown a booster twice. But the company had never attempted a Ship catch, which is a taller order, given how much faster and farther Starship upper stages fly.

So snagging Ship on the first try was a very massive deal, according to Musk.

"Everyone knew, within SpaceX, at least, how important this milestone was, and that it was really something fundamental and profound — that Starship will be the first-ever fully reusable orbital space system," he told Baker and Gracias on Wednesday.

Recent findings suggest that and SpaceX is very serious about Starship reuse. Musk has mentioned that the organization wants to launch about 10,000 Starship missions per year by 2030.

This mind-boggling cadence will help the company build out two enormous megaconstellations in low Earth orbit — the next iteration of its Starlink broadband network, which will consist of about 100,000 satellites, and its Starmind AI data-center constellation, which will be 10 times bigger than that.

Assembly of that fresh Starlink network is already underway. Ship carried 26 of the next-gen internet spacecraft up for the first time on Flight 14, which launched on Sept. 28, and repeated the feat on Flight 15.

#139184. Latest Update: Measles in America: Here's a constructive approach to beating the disease, based on Brazil's experience

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1406 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dw ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Measles in America: Here's a constructive approach to beating the disease, based on Brazil's experience

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1406 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Health experts saw it coming — the fact that after 26 years, the US would lose its status as measles-free.
  • On November 17, 2026, the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) noted the US had lost its measles elimination status, along with Mexico.
  • In a recent development, look at Brazil, where in 2019, with more than 21,000 measles cases, the country also lost its measles-free status.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Health experts saw it coming — the fact that after 26 years, the US would lose its status as measles-free. Back in July 2026, DW reported how one epidemiologist had suggested an 'amnesia' about the measles risk was pushing a growth in US infections.

Four months later, it was official. On November 17, 2026, the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) noted the US had lost its measles elimination status, along with Mexico.

But it doesn't have to stay this way.

In a recent development, look at Brazil, where in 2019, with more than 21,000 measles cases, the country also lost its measles-free status. But within five years — during the COVID-19 pandemic — it fought and won back its measles-free status. And since 2024, Brazil has stayed measles-free, even as the highly contagious disease spread across the rest of the Americas.

It has been revealed that in 2026, with the data available up to the time of writing this article, Brazil had only had 70 measles cases. They were all linked to infections brought in from abroad, often from neighboring Peru.

It has been revealed that brazil has fewer people than the US, about 213 million compared to the US's nearly 350 million, but the two countries are similar in size. So the comparison is worth considering.

In a recent development, brazil moves fast. The PAHO asks countries to respond within 72 hours of a suspected measles case. Here's Brazil's own rule:.

Recent findings suggest that it has also made hunting for cases a national habit. In a program called "Dia S," health workers knock on doors and visit schools, daycare centers and churches to find people who may be sick but have not seen a doctor.

Brazil also holds mass vaccination days called "Dia D." There was one in November, in the area where Brazil borders Colombia and Peru.

If someone is diagnosed with measles, health workers try to track down every person the patient may have met ("contact persons") and vaccinate them and other people living nearby.

The country has so far provided more than 16 million doses of the measles vaccine in 2026 and has donated 500,000 doses to Peru.

Industry observers note that brazil isn't perfect, though. According to official estimates from the World Health Organization, only 76% of children got both required doses of the vaccine in 2025 — well short of the 95% target. Experts warn this leaves the country at risk because measles is so highly contagious. A country needs to be as close to 100% immunized as possible to protect people and stop the disease from spreading.

"Elimination is not a trophy that we win once and put on a shelf. It must be protected every day," says PAHO Director Jarbas Barbosa.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

The US lost its measles-free status because the PAHO found that the same strain of the virus had been spreading in the country for 12 months or more. Mexico and Bolivia lost their status on the same day as the US.

In a recent development, the US has had more than 5,400 cases in 2026 (at time of writing), more than twice as many as in all of 2025, and about 19 times as many as in 2024. Nearly everyone who got sick with measles was unvaccinated or had an unknown vaccination status.

Recent findings suggest that US President Donald Trump signed an executive order on upcoming vaccination recommendations for children in August 2026. It came at a time, when, as we reported, experts mentioned people had stopped getting vaccinated against measles because infection rates were low. But like PAHO's Barbosa said, neglecting vaccination when infection rates are low is a mistake.

It has been revealed that to be fair, Trump's executive order listed the measles vaccine in a top category of vaccinations recommended for every child. But the administration's stance on vaccination in general is unclear.

Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has often declared opposition to vaccination, including against measles, advising people to take vitamin A instead. In Texas, this led to children being hospitalized with toxic levels of the supplement, and left them with no protection against measles.

Before the COVID-19 pandemic, 95% of US kindergartners had their measles shots. Now, it's 92%, according to the US Centers for Disease Control and Protection (CDC). That leaves about 280,000 kindergartners in the US unprotected.

In the Texas counties where a 2025 measles outbreak began, coverage was as low as 77% at the time.

US children usually need vaccines to start school, but most states let parents opt out for religious or personal reasons, with no doctor involved.

According to recent reports, but vaccination rates have fallen elsewhere in the world as well, including in Europe. In Germany, where measles infections have also risen, experts blame anti-vaccination rhetoric that emerged during the COVID-19 pandemic.

A person sick with measles can infect up to18 other, unprotected people. With vaccination, it is possible to increase the number of protected people and lower the number of people the sick person can infect.

According to recent reports, to prevent a measles outbreak, a community needs about 95% of people to be vaccinated and/or immune. The vaccination consists of two doses of the MMR (measles, mumps, rubella) vaccine.

But even after the two doses, a person can expect to have only 97% protection against measles — 3% short of full protection — so, nearly everyone in the community has to be vaccinated to keep the average level of protect as close to 100% as possible.

"For some diseases like measles, even a small decrease in vaccination rates can lead to more outbreaks of disease [so] community immunity requires over 95% of susceptible individuals to be immunized," says Andrew Racine, president of the American Academy of Pediatrics.

Recent findings suggest that and the 95% has to hold everywhere. A good national average can be affected by, for example, a single school where only 70% of the children are vaccinated. And that is where the outbreak is likely to start.

Around the world, measles deaths have dropped by 88% since 2000, thanks to vaccines.

But progress has stalled. Only about three out of four children worldwide get both doses of the vaccine. The biggest outbreaks right now are in Bangladesh, Indonesia and Guatemala.

Industry observers note that data from Europe indicates that things can get better. In the European Union, cases fell from more than 35,000 in 2024 to about 2,300 the following year, with no measles-related deaths.

Romania went from more than 30,000 cases in 2024 to about 4,200 in 2025.

In Hungary, where 99% of children are vaccinated, there have been no measles cases in the past year.

It has been revealed that but in January, six European countries lost their measles-free status, including the UK, Spain and Austria. Across Europe, eight out of ten people who got measles in 2025 were unvaccinated.

It has been revealed that the Americas are seeing a major surge in measles infections, with more than 58,000 cases in 2026, over four times as many as by November in 2025. Guatemala has been hit hardest, with almost 35,000 cases.

In a recent development, the deadliest outbreaks are in Africa. African Union countries have so far reported nearly 1,800 measles deaths in 2026, about 1,650 of them in Democratic Republic of Congo. Yet, Sudan, despite the war, raised first-dose measles coverage by 22 percentage points in 2025, which was the world's largest gain.

According to recent reports, measles is extremely contagious. One person can infect up to 18 unprotected people, which makes it about 12 times more contagious than the flu.

The virus can linger in the air for up to two hours after a sick person has left the room. And people spread it before they know they are sick. Someone with measles is contagious for four days before the rash appears and four days after.

Sources indicate that it's not just a rash. About one in five unvaccinated people who get measles in the US ends up in the hospital. Measles can weaken the immune system for years, making it harder to fight off other infections.

According to recent reports, but it's preventable. Two doses of the MMR vaccine (which also protects against mumps and rubella) protect 97% of people for life.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that grand Theft Auto VI (GTA 6) has been out for less than a week, but players have already found a plethora of considered details in the massive sandbox game.
  • According to recent reports, snapmatic is GTA 6's version of Instagram, filled with photos and memes reflecting the game's satirical rendition of the U.S.
  • As such, GTA 6 players have discovered that Snapmatic can be used to identify robbery targets.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that grand Theft Auto VI (GTA 6) has been out for less than a week, but players have already found a plethora of considered details in the massive sandbox game. Among them is a novel method players are using to get more money in GTA 6, helping them find robbery targets that are worth their time. It also doubles as an crucial reminder about internet safety.

According to recent reports, snapmatic is GTA 6's version of Instagram, filled with photos and memes reflecting the game's satirical rendition of the U.S. This includes people showing off drugs, cars, and weapons in a bid for clout. Like Instagram, Snapmatic also allows its fictional consumers to tag a location in their posts.

As such, GTA 6 players have discovered that Snapmatic can be used to identify robbery targets. Simply find a post with a location tagged, and open the menu you'd use to like it or view comments. Under the "Like" option will be "Set Destination," which will mark the location of the Snapmatic post on your map. You can then head there to relieve characters of their belongings (typically via the use of notable violence).

Sources indicate that it's an interesting gameplay mechanic that also serves as a reminder to be careful about what you post online. While the world of GTA 6 is a heightened version of reality, it does still have some basis in truth. There have been multiple real-life instances of criminals finding their victims via social media posts, something that's been occurring for years.

Last month, a UK man was convicted of stealing £48,000 (about $62,900) and various items from a home after seeing the family's social media posts indicating they'd be out hosting a Chinese Upcoming Year celebration. In 2021, four people were arrested in Italy for allegedly stealing from celebrities and influencers after monitoring their Instagram accounts, reportedly using victims' posts to identify tagged locations, entry points, and when they'd be away from home. Back in 2016, a California man was convicted of stealing personal items from female college students after finding them via GPS locations in photos posted to Instagram.

Even if you exclude location tags and don't mention your movements in your posts, you can still be vulnerable. Late last year, four French men travelled to Australia in order to rob a home of items reportedly valued at around $AU10 million ($6.6 million). According to court documents, the thieves saw photos of luxury goods that a victim had posted to Instagram, as well as images of their backyard and local surroundings. The thieves then used ChatGPT to search for where these pictures were taken, narrowing it down to a specific Australian city and suburb, which helped them locate the house.

According to recent reports, using social media to pick robbery targets in GTA 6 won't attract the same legal consequences and prison time that it would in real life. Rather, it serves as a neat little trick to help ambitious, self-starting criminals find worthwhile heists. However, this mechanic should also serve as an important reminder about the dangers of real-life Insta-bragging, and a warning to be careful about what you share online. #139182. Latest Update: Common medications may secretly rewire your gut, with effects lasting for years

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (863 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Common medications may secretly rewire your gut, with effects lasting for years

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (863 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Medications you stopped taking years ago may still be influencing the bacteria living in your gut.
  • It has been revealed that the gut microbiome is the vast community of bacteria and other microorganisms that inhabit the digestive tract.
  • Sources indicate that to investigate these connections, researchers examined stool samples and prescription histories from more than 2,500 participants in the Estonian Biobank's Estonian Microbiome cohort.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Medications you stopped taking years ago may still be influencing the bacteria living in your gut. A large study from the University of Tartu Institute of Genomics has found that many commonly prescribed drugs leave lasting changes in the gut microbiome, even long after people stop using them.

It has been revealed that the gut microbiome is the vast community of bacteria and other microorganisms that inhabit the digestive tract. These microbes play important roles in digestion, immune function, and overall health. While antibiotics are well known for disrupting gut bacteria, the new findings suggest that many other medications can also have effects that persist for years.

Sources indicate that to investigate these connections, researchers examined stool samples and prescription histories from more than 2,500 participants in the Estonian Biobank's Estonian Microbiome cohort. They discovered that most of the medications studied were associated with changes in gut bacteria. Even more surprisingly, a substantial number left detectable microbial "fingerprints" years after patients had stopped taking them.

Common Medications Leave Lasting Changes in Gut Bacteria.

Sources indicate that the findings extend far beyond antibiotics. Antidepressants, beta-blockers, proton pump inhibitors, and benzodiazepines were all linked to differences in the gut microbiome.

These medications are widely used to treat everyday health conditions. Beta-blockers are commonly prescribed for high blood pressure and certain heart conditions, while proton pump inhibitors reduce stomach acid and are frequently used to treat acid reflux. Benzodiazepines are often prescribed for anxiety, and antidepressants help manage depression and other mental health conditions.

"Most microbiome studies only consider current medications, but our results show that past drug use can be just as vital as it is a surprisingly strong factor in explaining individual microbiome differences," noted Dr. Oliver Aasmets, lead author.

This discovery suggests that looking only at the medications someone right now takes may overlook an crucial part of their gut health history. Previous prescriptions could help explain why the composition of gut bacteria differs so much from one person to another.

Anxiety Medications Show Effects Comparable to Antibiotics.

One of the most striking findings involved benzodiazepines, a class of medications commonly used to treat anxiety.

Recent findings suggest that researchers found that these drugs were associated with changes in the gut microbiome comparable to those seen with broad-spectrum antibiotics. These antibiotics target a wide variety of bacteria and are known to substantially alter the microbial communities living in the digestive system.

The researchers also discovered that medications within the same drug class did not necessarily produce the same effects. For example, diazepam and alprazolam are both benzodiazepines used to treat similar conditions, yet they appeared to differ in how strongly they disrupted gut bacteria.

This suggests that the effects of medication on the microbiome may depend not only on the type of drug being taken, but also on the specific medication.

Gut Bacteria Can Change When Medications Are Started or Stopped.

To investigate whether medications were actually contributing to these microbial changes, researchers collected additional stool samples from a smaller group of participants.

Industry observers note that by examining how the microbiome changed when people started or stopped certain medications, the team identified predictable shifts in gut bacteria. These findings provided additional evidence that the drugs themselves were contributing to the changes, rather than simply being associated with differences already present in patients.

According to recent reports, although the number of participants in this follow-up analysis was relatively small, the researchers were able to verify lasting effects associated with several drug categories. These included proton pump inhibitors, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, and certain antibiotics, including combinations of penicillins and macrolides.

Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, often called SSRIs, are a widely prescribed type of antidepressant. Macrolides are a class of antibiotics used to treat various bacterial infections.

Why Your Medication History May Matter More Than Previously Thought.

Recent findings suggest that the findings point to an crucial consideration for researchers studying the relationship between gut bacteria and disease. Differences in the microbiome may reflect not only a person's current health and medication use, but also treatments received years earlier.

If previous medications are not taken into account, scientists could mistakenly attribute certain microbial differences to a disease or another health factor when past drug exposure may have contributed.

The results also highlight how much remains to be understood about the long-term relationship between medications and the gut microbiome. Although the study identified persistent microbial changes, these findings do not establish that such changes are necessarily harmful or that they lead to specific health problems.

"This is a comprehensive systematic evaluation of long-term medication effects on the microbiome using real-world medical health records," said Professor Elin Org, corresponding author. "We hope this encourages researchers and clinicians to factor in medication history when interpreting microbiome data.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

LSU star Angel Reese defended the gesture she aimed at Iowa Hawkeyes’ Caitlin Clark near the end of the Tigers’ first NCAA women’s basketball national championship victory on Sunday, saying “I don’t take disrespect lightly.”.

Reese could be seen approaching Clark before moving her open hand in front of her face – popularized by WWE star John Cena to mean “you can’t see me” – before pointing to her ring finger in a gesture some interpreted as a reference to the place her newly-acquired championship ring might sit.

Caitlin Clark breaks records galore during historic March Madness run.

Clark made a similar gesture to another player earlier in the tournament.

It has been revealed that the gesture has sparked much debate, especially on social media. Some have criticized Reese, while others have defended her actions, highlighting how there was no public outrage in response to Clark’s gesture earlier in the tournament.

Sports journalist Jose de Jesus Ortiz called Reese’s actions “classless,” while former ESPN host Keith Olbermann called Reese an “idiot” for the gesture.

In the press conference after the victory, Reese referenced the difference in reaction she received as a result of her gesture as compared to the one Clark received.

Recent findings suggest that “All year, I was critiqued for who I was. I don’t fit the narrative,” Reese said. “I don’t fit the box that y’all want me to be in. I’m too hood. I’m too ghetto. Y’all told me that all year. But when other people do it, and y’all don’t say nothing.

“So this is for the girls that look like me. For those that want to speak up for what they believe in. It’s unapologetically you. And that’s what I did it for tonight. It was bigger than me tonight. And Twitter is going to go into a rage every time.

“And I’m happy. I feel like I’ve helped grow women’s basketball this year. (…) I’m looking forward to celebrating and then next season.”.

LSU beats Iowa to win its first NCAA women's basketball championship.

Reese had 15 points and 10 rebounds in the 102-85 victory and won the women’s March Madness’ Most Outstanding Player award.

In the post-game broadcast, Reese referenced the similar gesture Clark made to a Louisville opponent in the Elite Eight.

In the same game, Clark remarked to an opponent: “You’re down by 15 points. Shut up,” according to the Bleacher Report.

“Caitlin Clark is a hell of a player but I don’t take disrespect lightly,” Reese said. “She disrespected [LSU’s] Alexis [Morris] (…) and I wanted to pick her pocket. But I had a moment at the end of her game. I was in my bag, I was in my moment.”.

After the Championship game, Clark herself mentioned she didn’t notice anything at the time.

“I was just trying to get to the handshake line and shake hands and be grateful that my team was in that position,” Clark noted in the post-game press conference. “All the credit in the world to LSU. They were tremendous. They deserve it. They had a tremendous season.

“(LSU head coach) Kim Mulkey coached them so, so well. She’s one of the best basketball coaches of all time, and it shows. She only stated really kind things to me in the handshake line, so I’m very grateful of that too.

“But honestly I have no idea. I was just trying to spend the last few moments on the court with especially the five people that I’ve started 93 games with and relishing every second of that.”.

LSU head coach Mulkey noted she had “no clue” about what transpired.

Among those defending Reese on social media were ESPN’s Holly Rowe and former NBA star Etan Thomas.

Industry observers note that “People hating on Angel Reese or Caitlin Clark. Stop. Unapologetically confident young women should be celebrated NOT hated. Get used to it,” Rowe wrote on Twitter.

In a recent development, former Washington Wizards, Oklahoma City Thunder and Atlanta Hawks player Thomas wrote: “Hold on now!!!! It was cute when Caitlin Clark did it. Y’all didn’t have any issues with it at all. So don’t be all outraged and talking about class and sportsmanship when Angel Reese does the same thing. We’re not doing double standards here.”.

Reese said the negative reaction on social media throughout the season has helped fuel her excellent season, having finished averaging 23.0 points and 15.4 rebounds in her first season with LSU after transferring from Maryland.

Industry observers note that “Twitter can say what they want to say,” she mentioned. “I love reading those comments. I have all the screenshots of what everybody has said about me all season. What are you going to say now?”.

Under Byron Allen’s stewardship, we are confident we have the right elements in place to build BuzzFeed into a premier free-streaming service.”.

It has been revealed that debuted in 2006, BuzzFeed had become a buzzy upstart and hit a peak valuation of $1.7 billion in 2016. Among its investors was NBCUniversal, which pumped $400 million into the manufacturer. But BuzzFeed has seen its revenue crumble dramatically in recent years and has endured multiple rounds of layoffs. Currently, BuzzFeed has a market capitalization of under $40 million.

In a recent development, for the third quarter of 2026, BuzzFeed reported total revenue of $26.0 million (down 44%) and net loss of $18.7 million (versus a net loss of $7.4 million the year-earlier period). Allen, in announcing the results, mentioned Q3 was “a transitional quarter.”.

“The restructuring we announced in July reduced our workforce and dedicated contractors by approximately 35% and we expect this to yield approximately $30 million in annualized savings,” Allen stated. In the fourth quarter, “our strategy is to bring compelling content to audiences wherever they are — across digital platforms and connected TV — as we work to position BuzzFeed to be a premier global free streaming platform.”.

#139179. After 8 years in space, a groundbreaking X-ray telescope finally opens its eyes

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1598 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

After 8 years in space, a groundbreaking X-ray telescope finally opens its eyes

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1598 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • After eight years in space and a journey covering 10 billion kilometers, a pioneering X-ray telescope traveling to Mercury has captured its first observations of a distant cosmic object.
  • Scientists at the University of Leicester are now evaluating the Mercury Imaging X-ray Spectrometer (MIXS), which is traveling aboard the two-spacecraft mission.
  • Sources indicate that the telescope has spent eight years traveling through space, making it essential to confirm that its delicate components are still working properly.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After eight years in space and a journey covering 10 billion kilometers, a pioneering X-ray telescope traveling to Mercury has captured its first observations of a distant cosmic object. The instrument, built in the UK, successfully detected X-rays from the Crab Nebula, one of the brightest X-ray sources in the sky, marking an crucial milestone for the European Space Agency (ESA) and Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency's BepiColombo mission.

Scientists at the University of Leicester are now evaluating the Mercury Imaging X-ray Spectrometer (MIXS), which is traveling aboard the two-spacecraft mission. Their initial results are highly encouraging, arriving just as BepiColombo prepares to enter orbit around Mercury on November 21.

Sources indicate that the telescope has spent eight years traveling through space, making it essential to confirm that its delicate components are still working properly. Although engineers monitored MIXS throughout the journey, the instrument could not look directly into space until September. That opportunity came after the Mercury Transfer Module (MTM) separated from the two science orbiters, the Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO) and Mercury Magnetosphere Orbiter (MMO) or Mio.

With its view finally unobstructed, MIXS could begin the critical tests needed before the spacecraft enters its planned orbit around the solar system's smallest planet.

A Telescope's First Look Across 6,500 Light-Years.

Recent findings suggest that for its first astronomical target, the team selected the Crab Nebula, located approximately 6,500 light-years from Earth. This well-studied remnant of an exploded star produces a strong, predictable X-ray signal, making it an ideal reference for testing the telescope's performance.

Recent findings suggest that by examining how MIXS observes this distant object, researchers can determine whether the instrument still performs as expected after its lengthy journey. They can also compare the results with laboratory measurements collected in 2015, when the telescope was last tested on Earth.

In a recent development, the main observation campaign took place on September 11 and 12. Over 39 hours, the spacecraft carried out 55 carefully controlled changes in orientation to collect the data.

It has been revealed that one important measurement was the telescope's angular resolution, which describes its ability to distinguish small details in an image. Scientists determined this by examining how widely the Crab Nebula's X-ray signal spread across the detector. Remarkably, MIXS delivered slightly sharper resolution than it had during its laboratory tests in 2015.

That improvement is particularly encouraging because the instrument will eventually use its X-ray vision to investigate the composition of Mercury's surface.

Better Than Expected After Eight Years in Space.

Professor Emma Bunce, Principal Investigator (PI) for MIXS and Director of the Institute for Space at the University of Leicester, welcomed the results as a major achievement for the international team responsible for developing the instrument.

Professor Bunce noted: "We have waited a long time to make measurements with MIXS and it is fantastic to see it operating brilliantly in space. This is testament to our engineering and technical team, and our international partners who we have worked with over many years to build this incredible instrument. 80% of the technology on MIXS is latest!

It has been revealed that "During our calibration observations we have determined that MIXS is generally performing fantastically well in space! We have no effects in our images that are associated with 'stray light' (optical photons getting in when they should not). We continue to see effects of galactic cosmic rays as we did during cruise, but we understand these and can filter them out. We see some self-fluorescence which appears when the Sun is illuminating the optic, but this won't affect our dayside observations of Mercury's surface. And the detector has suffered no radiation damage after 8 years in space.

"We see some effects in the instrument that we are still studying and expect to undertake some optimization procedures during the Mercury commissioning phase to fine tune MIXS in preparation for the science phase.".

The results suggest that the telescope has weathered its long exposure to the harsh space environment exceptionally well. Engineers have found no unwanted visible light interfering with its images, and the effects of high-energy cosmic rays are understood well enough to be removed during data processing.

Sources indicate that the team has also identified a small amount of X-ray emission originating within the instrument itself when sunlight strikes its optics. However, this effect is not expected to interfere with observations of Mercury's sunlit surface. Most importantly, the detector indicates no signs of radiation damage after eight years in space.

Some remaining effects still require investigation, and scientists expect to make further adjustments after the spacecraft reaches Mercury to ensure that MIXS is ready for its full scientific mission.

How X-Rays Will Reveal Mercury's Hidden Chemistry.

BepiColombo is designed to investigate Mercury in unprecedented detail. As the smallest and one of the least explored rocky planets in our solar system, Mercury offers scientists a rare opportunity to understand how planets form and change under the extreme conditions found close to a star.

One of the mission's major goals is to uncover the planet's chemical composition and geological history. These findings could help explain Mercury's unusual characteristics while providing broader insights into the formation and evolution of the solar system.

In a recent development, MIXS, carried aboard the Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO), will play a central role in this investigation. Developed by a European consortium led by the University of Leicester, it draws on the university's long history of X-ray astronomy research.

It is the first imaging X-ray telescope to operate on a planetary science mission. Working alongside other scientific instruments, MIXS will help produce a global map showing the elements that make up Mercury's surface, revealing its atomic composition in greater detail than ever before. It is also the only UK-led scientific instrument aboard BepiColombo and receives support from the UK Space Agency.

The instrument works by detecting fluorescent X-rays released by rocks on Mercury's surface. When powerful X-rays from the Sun strike these rocks, they can cause atoms within the material to emit X-rays of their own. Different elements produce characteristic X-ray signals, allowing scientists to identify what the surface is made of without collecting physical samples.

MIXS will make these measurements with assistance from the Solar Intensity X-ray and particle Spectrometer (SIXS), which monitors the solar radiation and particles reaching Mercury.

The telescope will also examine X-rays emitted from Mercury's nighttime surface when charged particles associated with the planet's magnetic environment strike it. These measurements could reveal important connections between Mercury's surface and the surrounding space environment.

A 10 Billion Kilometer Journey With a Personal Legacy.

For Dr. Adrian Martindale, MIXS Instrument Scientist at the University of Leicester's School of Physics and Astronomy, the successful observations represent the culmination of more than two decades of work.

Martindale joined the project in 2003 while still an undergraduate student and has been involved in nearly every aspect of the instrument's development.

Sources indicate that dr. Martindale remarked: "BepiColombo, and MIXS in particular, are like part of my family. I've been involved since I was an undergraduate and touched almost every part of the instrument before it was debuted.

Recent findings suggest that "This first data is mind-blowing to me. The last time we could see through this telescope it was in the basement under the School of Physics and Astronomy in Leicester, but after a rocket launch, eight years in space and 10 billion kilometers traveled it looks just the same. I can't wait to see the science data it produces when we get into orbit.".

The milestone also carries special meaning for the team because MIXS represents the scientific legacy of Professor George Fraser. Fraser was the instrument's original Principal Investigator and the driving force behind its innovative optical design before his death in March 2014.

Professor Bunce added: "We are thinking of George as we operate MIXS fully in space for the first time and know that he would be very, very proud of the team and delighted at our first light observations.".

BepiColombo Prepares for Its Final Arrival at Mercury.

BepiColombo began its arrival phase on September 3, when the Mercury Transfer Module (MTM) separated from the spacecraft assembly.

The remaining connected spacecraft are scheduled to enter orbit around Mercury on November 21. The two science orbiters, MPO and Mio, are then expected to separate on December 9 to 10, allowing them to prepare for their respective scientific operations.

The mission's primary science phase is scheduled to begin in April 2027. Once underway, BepiColombo will investigate Mercury's surface, internal structure, magnetic field, and surrounding environment, helping scientists piece together the history of a planet that remains surprisingly mysterious despite its proximity to the Sun.

For the MIXS team, the successful first observations of the Crab Nebula offer an early indication of what the instrument may accomplish when it finally turns its attention to Mercury.

International Collaboration and Funding.

Industry observers note that MIXS was developed through a partnership involving research institutions and technology companies across Europe. Participating organizations include:.

UK funding for the BepiColombo MIXS instrument comes from the UK Space Agency, which serves as the lead funding organization, along with STFC, the European Space Agency, and the University of Leicester.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, more than a year after KPop Demon Hunters became a global sensation — a human-made antidote to the AI slop flooding the Internet — billion-dollar hits like Toy Story 5 and The Super Mario Galaxy Movie and acclaimed work like Wildwood, Flow, Blue Eye Samurai, Arcane and X-Men ’97 make the case that the human touch is still what moves animation audiences. Breaking in, though, has never been harder. The studio system is contracting, AI threatens to rewire production pipelines, and latest platforms and producers (see: YouTube and Glitch) are redrawing the map.

Recent findings suggest that professional connections, fearless experimentation and creative innovation are key. Animation schools play a critical role, preparing emerging talent to be ready on day one to build upon existing pipelines of voices and projects that’ll define the industry’s next chapter. “The great thing about the industry is that because it’s made up of artists, it’s first and foremost a meritocracy,” notes Sam Goff, animation talent manager, recruiter and educator. “Networking and industry access also play a huge part, but you could have all the connections in the world, and if you don’t have the skills and can’t actually do the work, you’re not getting hired.” Related Stories Movies Hailee Steinfeld on Recording Music for Fresh Movie 'Hexed' and Becoming a Mother in the Process Movies Magnolia Pictures Takes French Animated Gay Comedy 'Jim Queen' for U.S.

Sources indicate that THR names the top U.S. schools where animation’s next gen can do just that — build their skills, professionally network and gain necessary industry access.

In a recent development, this program is about mastering teamwork and production so students can integrate seamlessly into 2D and 3D studio pipelines. Across its two colleges and three departments, Pixar, DreamWorks and Sony Animation veterans deliver a generalist approach that embraces arts and technology coursework while encouraging development in a single expertise. Professional development opportunities span internships at Disney Feature Animation and Lucas Arts/ILM, career and business strategy courses, and an annual student film created by the graduating class (2026’s Dungeons & Dragons-inspired Love & Gold won a student Emmy). This year, a latest arts building also added classrooms, computer labs, theaters, postproduction facilities and production stage access through a BYU Film collaboration.

TUITION $7,096 (Church of Latter-Day Saints members); $14,192 (non-LDS members).

ALUMNI Jake Wyatt (My Adventures With Superman).

In a recent development, the storied CalArts offers courses tied to animation history, theory, screenwriting, character design, sound and, yes, Disney movies, in classes that are small and taught entirely by working artists. The Patty Disney Center for Life and Work uses a mix of support — one-on-one career advising, an entrepreneurial incubator program, a career and opportunity festival, animation portfolio day, weekly guest speakers and a robust internship program. The approach has produced talent like experimental animator and Oscar nominee Siqi Song (Sister) and Lindsay Scanlan, whose fourth-year film went viral before she was hired for the Disney Channel series The Ghost and Molly McGee.

ALUMNI Sean Buckelew (Common Side Effects); Glen Keane (The Little Mermaid).

In a recent development, boasting 13 scholarships, the School of Art’s diverse and industry-adjacent program is an affordable option for learning animated filmmaking or preproduction. Led by faculty who’ve worked on King of the Hill and at Disneyland Paris, students are exposed to studio art and a breadth of animation forms alongside internships at studios like Titmouse and Bento Box, with recent graduates hired at MrBeast and HBO. This year, students will produce an animated short in collaboration with the U.N., and a new animation incubator — released in partnership with ASIFA-Hollywood — will bring alums and other industry talent to campus, offering students mentorship and production opportunities on innovative shorts tackling social activism and cutting-edge technologies.

TUITION $3,419 (in-state); $10,017 (out-of-state).

ALUMNI Daniel Chong (Hoppers); Theresa Reyes (Toy Story 4).

Recent findings suggest that dePaul’s breadth of concentrations are taught by a large, full-time faculty, with access to animators in residence like Brian Ferguson (The Lion King, Mulan). Student orgs connect with Chicago’s animation community, and there are practical courses, such as one co-created and run by Nickelodeon Animation directors that taught the studio’s process for storyboarding the show SpongeBob SquarePants. An L.A.-focused internship program brings DePaul to Hollywood, with work at ShadowMachine and the Jim Henson Co. This year, the school expanded the capabilities of its virtual production LED Volume with enhanced motion-capture systems, introduced an animation cohort to its six-week summer Chicago Housing Authority program, and offered new career development opportunities with visual effects company DNEG and through a Film + Animation Industry Night.

TUITION $48,180 (undergraduate); $1,003 per credit hour (graduate).

ALUMNI Molly McCandless (Wildwood), Sebastian Newell (Nickelodeon + CBS Animation Studios).

Industry observers note that those with a strong portfolio, unique personal perspective and penchant for experimentation will find a home in the Illustration and Film/Animation/Video (FAV) program, which boasts a more than 90 percent freshman retention and school graduation rate despite its famously intensive coursework. Graduates of RISD’s animation-related undergraduate and graduate degrees, which combine arts and liberal arts studies, frequently leave their mark as independent entrepreneurs or in studio work like directing, writing, animating, character designing and producing at such companies as Pixar, DreamWorks, HBO and PBS. This year, FAV’s course catalog expanded to include production design, live-action puppetry and other multidisciplinary, design-driven courses, while the school hosted the inaugural symposium for its recently launched Movement Lab in October.

ALUMNI Michaela Olsen and Emily Collins (Mighty Oak studio).

Alongside alumni speakers like Diane Ikemiyashiro, a vp at Disney Junior, and Hotel Transylvania 5 co-director Alan Hawkins, students are educated by faculty with credits on Avatar: Fire and Ash and Stranger Things: Tales From ’85 in a rigorous curriculum spanning foundational art and the animation pipeline. A pre-college program unlocks access to financial aid before enrolling, while current students and recent alums have secured internships or work at Pixar, DreamWorks, Sony and Netflix Animation. Its new 2D Character Animation B.F.A. will also help students develop the artistic, technical and entrepreneurial foundation needed for today’s evolving animation industry, whether working at a major studio, in a freelance career or launching a creator-owned indie production.

ALUMNI Michael Yates (Incredibles 3); Michelle Cowart (Forgotten Island).

In a recent development, for a cutting-edge institution offering the latest animation tools and techniques with a well-connected alumni network, look to SCAD’s School of Animation and Motion or collaborative programs in interactive design and game development, themed entertainment design and illustration at the Savannah and Atlanta campuses. In the past five years, students have participated in screenings and master classes, been hired at Laika and Sony Pictures Imageworks, and interned at Disney Imagineering and Steamroller Animation. Alongside alumni working on three of 2026’s best animation Oscar nominees, student animated films have earned more than 400 official selections and recognitions, including the Student Academy Awards, College Television Awards and Cannes Indie Shorts Awards.

TUITION $42,975 (undergraduate); $43,965 (graduate).

ALUMNI Zach Parrish (The Sea Beast); Vinod Krishnan (The Simpsons).

Sources indicate that emerging artists — including Pell-qualifying graduates of New York City high schools awarded a minimum $30,000 annually as incoming freshmen — can access undergrad and grad programs that support the mastery of the entire 3D and VFX pipeline, foundational art, animation history, specialization training and short-film production. Its classes hone students’ animation, motion design or experimental art visions. Students have access to state-of-the-art and industry-standard software and gear, as well as labs supporting sound, motion-capture, stop-motion and pencil work. That’s alongside a pre-college program; the SVA in L.A. networking program; studio visits to Walt Disney Animation; portfolio reviews by Pixar and Skydance employees; lectures and workshops with WIA, VES, SIGGRAPH and ASIFA; a senior industry networking mixer; and career courses, including pilot writing and pitching techniques.

TUITION $27,635 (undergraduate); $30,845 (graduate).

ALUMNI Vivienne Medrano (Hazbin Hotel); Enrico Casarosa (Luca).

Sources indicate that with a 5-to-1 student-to-teacher ratio, access to live-action electives and funding support like the Matt Groening Production Fellowship in Animation, the school’s M.F.A. via the Animation Workshop offers a distinctly intimate pathway to learning every phase of filmmaking through the lens of animation. At the school, founded in 1948 by former Disney animator Bill Shull, students complete three films while learning from artists like Phoebe & Jay co-creator Thy Than and interning at studios like Starburns Industries. This year, they also heard from alums on DreamWorks Animation’s Forgotten Island and benefited from the addition of four full-body and facial motion-capture systems and an eMotimo Spectrum ST4 to support student work in stop-motion.

TUITION $13,722 (in-state); $25,967 (out-of-state).

ALUMNI Latoya Raveneau (The Proud Family: Louder and Prouder).

What do Hexed, Shrek 5, The Cat in the Hat and GOAT have in common? All four have USC faculty on their crews. With working artists running the classes, the curriculum keeps pace with the industry, with a focus on creation, design, innovation and cross-industry collaboration. Alongside efforts like Studio Day, which attracts 20-plus companies for interviews and portfolio reviews, faculty walk students through the applications, interviews and contract negotiations. The programs’ success is evidenced by 2025 graduates like Pablo Diaz De Leon Hicks and Matthew Sorgie, both selected for the 2026 American Pavilion Emerging Filmmaker Showcase at Cannes.

TUITION $75,384 (undergraduate); $61,299 (graduate).

ALUMNI Andrew Millstein (Annapurna Animation); Lori Forte (Ice Age).

9 OTHER SCHOOLS TO WATCH THANKS TO DISTINCT OPPORTUNITIES AND PARTNERSHIPS.

When Amy Hurwitz, a veteran of LAIKA’s recruitment team, reached out to Bowie State University about a potential partnership around the start of the pandemic, Tewodross Melchishua Williams, professor, program and internship coordinator for the school’s Department of Fine and Performing Arts, was “immediately excited about what that could mean for our students,” he says. “HBCUs have extraordinary talent, but we don’t always have the same access to specialized facilities, equipment, funding, or direct industry relationships as other institutions.”.

The partnership with the Oregon-based studio helps close some of those gaps, offering the students in Visual Communication and Digital Media Arts (VCDMA) access to Bowie’s first stop-motion course. Through it, around 20 students annually learn sculpture, cinematography, fabrication, and storytelling alongside character and puppet design, set construction and lighting, frame-by-frame animation, and post-production.

Sources indicate that the school is also now home to Studio Ayoka Chenzira, funded by LAIKA and named in honor of Dr. Ayoka Chenzira, a pioneering filmmaker, animator, and department chair at Spelman College. “For me, that name matters,” claims Williams. “It connects the space to an African American woman whose work helped expand what animation and experimental filmmaking could be, and it gives our students a legacy to learn from.”.

Sources indicate that both initiatives have unlocked access to industry professionals, professional workflows, summer intensive workshops, and internship opportunities, with this year’s LAIKA movie Wildwood counting three very recent alumni as either crew or interns. “I tell students that talent matters, but so does curiosity, discipline, collaboration, and professionalism,” the Bowie State professor says. “Seeing our alumni contribute to a feature like Wildwood makes those lessons tangible.”.

For LAIKA, the partnership has resulted in more facilities and access to “talented emerging artists whose backgrounds and perspectives can broaden the field,” indicates Williams. “The industry needs technical skill, absolutely, but it also needs more voices and different perspectives.”.

The collaboration has also inspired similar efforts, like a partnership between Gobelins Paris, Netflix, and Guillermo del Toro, with the support of animation studio ShadowMachine. These serve as “a powerful reminder of the artistry, patience, and human craftsmanship at the heart of animation” in the age of AI, notes Williams. “For students, that’s an notable lesson: even as technology changes, foundational skills in movement, design, lighting, storytelling, and collaboration remain essential.”.

Below, THR looks at other schools with distinct parnterships and opportunities.

Creative Network: At Loyola Marymount University, faculty member Sydney Bright, head of global animation at WEBTOON Productions, leads a Studio Development Series for animated content. At NYU, home to The Jeff Baena Award, an undergraduate production scholarship supporting advanced-level projects, Nickelodeon’s senior vice president, TV series animation, Claudi Spinelli serves as one of the Animation Alumni Association’s founding members.

Industry observers note that gamers Gateway: Rochester Institute of Technology is home to Magic Spell Studios, out of which the student-run Overshoot Animation Productions supports the development of indie games, films and animated series. And Texas A&M’s programs support research in game-based learning and direct partnerships with studios like ProbablyMonsters at the Fort Worth Visualization campus.

In a recent development, local Connections: Through Kansas City Art Institute’s Sponsored Studio program, animation students created a 22-episode series for the Kansas City Royals Dominican Academy. At Massachusetts College of Art and Design, emerging animators can team with students at the Berklee College of Music to help their projects receive top level musical scores.

Universe Building: The B.F.A.’s story emphasis offers specialization specifically in animation story development while the Otis x Pixar Story Workshop lets selected students experience a studio-level story development process. The University of Central Florida’s Emerging Media B.F.A. Animation and Visualization track develops storytelling and animation skills around themed entertainment, with numerous professional development opportunities via the UCF/Universal Creative Lab partnership.

Latest Update: 'Star Trek: First Contact' at 30: Resistance is futile when it comes to the 'Next Generation' crew's greatest massive-screen adventure

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1898 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Space

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that following the sad news of Sir Patrick Stewart's passing, there's been no shortage of discussion about his best moments as Captain Jean-Luc Picard.
  • Recent findings suggest that with the Borg overrunning the newly released USS Enterprise-E, Picard — who has long-standing beef with the Collective, following his assimilation in classic "The Next Generation" story "The Best of Both Worlds" — orders his crew to fight the cybernetic nasties hand-to-hand if required, defying their pleas to activate the ship's self-destruct system and retreat.
  • It has been revealed that but following some impassioned talk about making the Borg "pay for what they've done", he's finally talked down from his rage by 21st-century stowaway Lily Sloane (Alfre Woodard).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that following the sad news of Sir Patrick Stewart's passing, there's been no shortage of discussion about his best moments as Captain Jean-Luc Picard. "The Inner Light"'s life in 25 minutes is a strong contender, as are the courtroom grandstanding in "The Measure of a Man" and his insistence (under extreme torture) that "there are four lights!" in "Chain of Command". But for this writer's money, it's hard to look past a nine-minute sequence in "Star Trek: First Contact", which turns 30 this weekend.

Recent findings suggest that with the Borg overrunning the newly released USS Enterprise-E, Picard — who has long-standing beef with the Collective, following his assimilation in classic "The Next Generation" story "The Best of Both Worlds" — orders his crew to fight the cybernetic nasties hand-to-hand if required, defying their pleas to activate the ship's self-destruct system and retreat. He even calls Worf — not a man renowned for dodging a fight — a coward, prompting the Klingon to respond that, "If you were any other man, I would kill you where you stand." Ouch.

It has been revealed that but following some impassioned talk about making the Borg "pay for what they've done", he's finally talked down from his rage by 21st-century stowaway Lily Sloane (Alfre Woodard). She points out that his Moby-Dick-esque obsession is on the verge of going full Ahab, and he eventually sees sense, issuing the order to abandon the Enterprise and destroy the hive.

It has been revealed that it's a masterclass showcasing the ever-brilliant Stewart's impressive range, as the out-of-control captain's rarely seen temper reaches fever pitch, before normal service is resumed. His subsequent apology to Worf — "As a matter of fact, I think you're the bravest man I've ever known" — is simply perfect.

And just as the franchise's zenith, "The Wrath of Khan", is built around Kirk and Khan's decades-old feud, "First Contact" is precision engineered to get the most out of Jean-Luc. This was the right "Star Trek" at the right time, a film that put "TNG"'s greatest villains on a collision course with the origins of Starfleet. It's not quite "Khan", of course — what is? — but it deserves to be mentioned in the same breath.

In 1996, the "odd numbers bad, even numbers good" rule of "Trek" films still, more or less, rang true. 1994's "Generations", rushed out a few months after "The Next Generation" ended its seven-year run on TV, had done decent business, but the seventh movie's convoluted "passing the baton" storyline had left many fans cold. Now, however, with Kirk killed off, it was time for Picard and his crew to explore the big-screen frontier alone.

William Shatner actually pitched a resurrection storyline for Kirk, but "Trek" executive producer/overlord Rick Berman ruled that it was a little too soon to bring the good captain back. Instead, he hired "Generations" scripters and "TNG"/"Deep Space Nine" writers' room regulars Brannon Braga and Ronald D. Moore to craft an eighth movie capable of living up to its even-numbered predecessors.

While "Generations" had been written to an extremely restrictive brief, Braga and Moore were given much more freedom the second time out. Berman was keen on a time-travel storyline while Braga lobbied for the fan-favorite Borg, and early on they explored the idea of taking the Collective back to Renaissance Italy. These intends were abandoned when Stewart vetoed the idea of wearing tights.

They eventually zeroed in on April 5, 2063, the date Zefram Cochrane (a character who'd previously appeared in Original Series episode "Metamorphosis") made humanity's first warp flight and put Earth on the radar of a passing Vulcan ship.

"We landed on the idea of what I called the 'Star Trek' nativity scene — the birth of 'Star Trek'," Braga said in "The Fifty-Year Mission" by Mark A Altman and Edward Gross.

It has been revealed that "The three wise Vulcans who arrive on Earth and step out of their ship for our first contact with an extraterrestrial species. And the Borg were going to prevent that from happening, which really struck a bullseye for me, because it would allow non-'Star Trek' people to understand why 'Star Trek' matters by putting the crew and the Borg back in that time frame. I thought it would appeal to a larger audience. 'Star Trek' itself was at stake, and that was super cool to me.".

Paramount reportedly flirted with significant-name directors like Ridley Scott ("Alien", "Blade Runner") and John McTiernan ("Predator", "Die Hard"), before settling on Jonathan Frakes. Although this would be Frakes' first movie, the man best known for playing Commander Riker had directed numerous "Trek" episodes. Berman believed that an understanding of the franchise's DNA was more important than big-screen experience.

The film wastes little time on exposition for "Trek" newbies, with just a short dream sequence to explain away Picard's history with the Borg. With a single Borg Cube on course for Earth, the Federation fleet mobilizes to fight them off. They're getting their asses well and truly kicked, too, until the Enterprise warps into the battle.

It has been revealed that the Cube is ultimately destroyed but still manages to dispatch a Sphere, which uses chronometric particles to travel back to 2063 in order to assimilate Earth in the past. Picard has no choice but to follow them back to "repair whatever damage they've done".

Industry observers note that they arrive in a post-World War III Montana, where Cochrane has constructed his prototype faster-than-light vessel, the Phoenix. Played by "Babe" star James Cromwell (who'd already guest-starred in a trio of "TNG" episodes), Cochrane is some way from the man future history has remembered: a hard-drinking womanizer more motivated by potential riches than the betterment of mankind. A man uncomfortable with the idea that a high school will one day bear his name.

But as some of the crew work to repair the damage caused by the Sphere's bombing raid, there are bigger problems in orbit. Borg survivors have beamed on board the Enterprise and started assimilating the vessel and its crew.

Industry observers note that initial drafts of the script saw Riker leading the ship-based resistance while Picard remained on Earth, but — at Stewart's request — Braga and Moore flipped things round to bring the captain face-to-face with his nemesis. It proved to be a really smart move, as Stewart got to ditch his upcoming-look Starfleet uniform and run around the Enterprise as a full-on action hero in a John McClane-style vest.

According to recent reports, these Borg had been given a multiplex upgrade, with massively improved prosthetics and newly introduced extendable tendrils that injected nanoprobes to assimilate a victim from within. Frakes played up the horror aspects of the Collective, portraying them as a horde of mindless cybernetic zombies, while using "Alien" and "Aliens" as inspiration.

Industry observers note that "[Ridley Scott and James Cameron] made it clear that when it comes to villains, the more that's suggested, the scarier they are," Frakes explained. "I tried to get that with the Borg.".

The biggest change came at the head of the organization, where — at the suggestion of Paramount executive Jonathan Dolgen — "First Contact" introduced a previously unseen Borg Queen (brilliantly played by Alice Krige) to act as spokesperson for the Collective.

Bringing a singular entity to a civilisation built on the notion that there's no "I" in "team" was a controversial move, but it made perfect dramatic sense. Indeed, a legion of drones would have little chance of seducing Data, even if it was just for 0.68 seconds.

Sources indicate that "We wrestled with it quite a bit before we committed to [the Borg Queen's] character," Moore told Syfy Wire, "because it was a choice that was also antithetical to the idea of the Borg. The whole concept of these villains was that they were a collection, and that there were no individuals. And that's what made them the faceless, implacable 'resistance is futile' enemy. But it also limited how to deal with them dramatically because it meant that any scenes you always had to deal with this sort of collective voice. We decided that the story would be better if we had some individual to deal with.".

The Queen was also granted one of the greatest entrances in sci-fi history, as her head and torso were lowered into a robot body with a bit of help from Industrial Light & Magic.

It has been revealed that the Starfleet armada's assault on the Borg was similarly impressive and effectively a test run for "The Phantom Menace", as ILM's visual effects supervisor John Knoll pioneered the CG effects pipeline that would later become pivotal to the "Star Wars" prequels. It was also a brilliant excuse to introduce several fresh starship designs to the "Trek" canon.

Sources indicate that they're standout moments in a film that made the most of its comparatively puny budget of $45 million (reported). (For comparison, "Independence Day", which was released the same year — and also featured Brent Spiner — cost closer to $75 million.).

As Moore later recalled in an interview with the Hollywood Reporter, "Paramount had their formula. They said that 'Star Trek' movies only make this amount of money. So, therefore, you can only have this amount of budget to make it. And, at that point, we were still — just like on the TV show — counting phaser beam effects shots [to keep the price down].".

Sources indicate that the studio needn't have worried. "First Contact" was a huge hit with fans and became one of the franchise's highest-grossing films at the box office. Borg mythology introduced here (including the Queen) would become a mainstay on "Star Trek: Voyager", while Jean-Luc would get to face his cybernetic white whale again in "Picard" — though the incomparable Stewart arguably never again had another "Trek" scene to rival the ones he had here.

Industry observers note that "Fortunately it happened to be a wonderful script, and my job was not to screw it up," mentioned Frakes. "It also holds up as a movie that just happens to be a 'Star Trek' movie, which we were all hoping would be the case.".

'Star Trek: First Contact' is available to stream on Paramount+ in the US and the UK.

Richard's love affair with outer space started when he saw the original "Star Wars" on TV aged four, and he spent much of the ’90s watching "Star Trek”, "Babylon 5” and “The X-Files" with his mum. After studying physics at university, he became a journalist, swapped science fact for science fiction, and hit the jackpot when he joined the team at SFX, the UK's biggest sci-fi and fantasy magazine. He liked it so much he stayed there for 12 years, four of them as editor.

He's since gone freelance and passes his time writing about "Star Wars", "Star Trek" and superheroes for the likes of SFX, Total Film, TechRadar and GamesRadar+. He has met five Doctors, two Starfleet captains and one Luke Skywalker, and once sat in the cockpit of "Red Dwarf"'s Starbug.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Robert Pattinson has been cast as the next James Bond in the upcoming film from director Denis Villeneuve.
  • Pattinson will be the seventh actor to play the role.
  • "James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honour of a lifetime," Pattinson said in a statement.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Robert Pattinson has been cast as the next James Bond in the upcoming film from director Denis Villeneuve. It will be the 26th James Bond film and the first since Amazon MGM took over the iconic franchise.

Pattinson will be the seventh actor to play the role. Monday's announcement — which came in part via an Instagram post — ends a long period of speculation about who would take over as "007" after Daniel Craig.

"James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honour of a lifetime," Pattinson said in a statement. "I couldn't be more excited about this partnership and the work ahead with this fantastic team.".

Recent findings suggest that pattinson has appeared in several substantial-ticket films this year, including Christopher Nolan's "The Odyssey" and psychological thriller "Primetime," and he'll soon appear in "Dune: Part Three," also directed by Villeneuve. Pattinson, who rose to fame with the Twilight movie series, is also in production for Matt Reeves' "The Batman Part II," a follow-up to the 2022 film based on the DC comic.

The upcoming Bond film will have a script by Steven Knight and will be produced by Amy Pascal, known for her work on the Spider-Man franchise, and David Heyman, who produced all eight Harry Potter films.

Sources indicate that "We were surrounded by extraordinary talent, but there can only be one 007," Villeneuve stated. "I am overjoyed to welcome Robert Pattinson as our upcoming James Bond. He has the timeless soul of 007 and brings a spirit that is completely new. I cannot wait to begin.".

Recent findings suggest that in 2022, Amazon bought MGM Studios, which had long produced the Bond movies, for roughly $8.45 billion. Amazon MGM then acquired creative control of the James Bond intellectual property rights in 2025, when it closed a deal with longtime producers Barbara Broccoli and Michael G. Wilson.

The film is still untitled, and Amazon MGM hasn't unveiled a projected release date.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • According to recent reports, in-game social media app Snapmatic is GTA 6's version of Instagram, offering a scrollable feed of posts from fictional characters showing off their very lootable possessions.
  • Players swiftly took note of GTA 6's memes, praising them for accurately capturing the irreverent vibe and frequently off-colour humour that typically characterises such media.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA 6) offers a satirical rendition of the U.S., filled with cars, crime, and shenanigans worthy of the game's Florida-inspired setting. It also incorporates many digital elements of modern life, including social media. Of course, where there's social media, there are inevitably memes.

According to recent reports, in-game social media app Snapmatic is GTA 6's version of Instagram, offering a scrollable feed of posts from fictional characters showing off their very lootable possessions. However, Snapmatic isn't just filled with posts sharing potential theft coordinates. It also contains a plethora of memes specifically created to populate GTA 6's social media.

Players swiftly took note of GTA 6's memes, praising them for accurately capturing the irreverent vibe and frequently off-colour humour that typically characterises such media.

"GTA 6 is so realistic that I thought this was a real meme," posted X user @thisdopenose, sharing an image of an in-game meme. In the meme, the text "bisexuals when they realise you can have sex more than twice" is edited onto a monochrome image of a man crying. The popular post has 94,000 likes at time of writing.

"They need to give a pay rise to whoever came up with the shitposts on Snapmatic bro these things are so funny," wrote @vandalfeet.

Some of GTA 6's in-game memes even referred to memes about GTA 6 itself. It's been 13 years since GTA 5 introduced, with many fans having eagerly awaited the franchises' latest instalment for over a decade. In the interim, it became a common meme for people to jokingly express disbelief that various other events had occurred "before GTA 6" arrived.

It has been revealed that developer Rockstar Games appears to have been aware of such memes, creating its own versions referring to GTA 6's fictional video game Race and Chase 7. ("Race'n'Chase" was the original working title for the first Grand Theft Auto game released in 1997).

Rockstar Games had teams dedicated to creating in-game media, aiming to flesh out GTA 6's world and make it feel more immersive. Judging by fans' reactions, it appears to have paid off. Parent company Take-Two Interactive estimates that GTA 6 achieved $3.79 billion in sales on day one alone, making it one of the biggest entertainment media introduces ever. Can German auto manufacturing recover after Mercedes and VW cuts?

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (886 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Mercedes-Benz's announcement last week that it would halt further investments at its factories in Germany has added to the sense that the country's best automaking days are behind it.
  • In a written interview for staff, production chief Michael Schiebe noted how the running costs of German plants are far too high.
  • Schiebe added that the automaker is "now forced to carefully examine which German sites we would have to close if we cannot achieve a change in the cost structure.".
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mercedes-Benz's announcement last week that it would halt further investments at its factories in Germany has added to the sense that the country's best automaking days are behind it.

In a written interview for staff, production chief Michael Schiebe noted how the running costs of German plants are far too high.

Schiebe added that the automaker is "now forced to carefully examine which German sites we would have to close if we cannot achieve a change in the cost structure.".

The decision came one day after Volkswagen (VW), Europe's largest carmaker, stated it was shelving aims to modernize its massive Wolfsburg plant.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Recent findings suggest that germany's auto sector is in a deep crisis, amid fierce rivalry from ambitious Chinese automakers. VW alone is looking to cut 100,000 jobs globally by 2030, while four of its German factories are earmarked for possible closure.

Yet, many auto analysts doubt this really marks the beginning of the end for car making in the country.

Sources indicate that "We have to admit that a third of our capacity [in German plants] is overcapacity and that needs to be cut," Thomas Puls, senior economist for transport and infrastructure at the Cologne Institute for Economic Research (IW Köln), told DW. "This will hurt a lot.".

A report last month by Munich-based consultancy Roland Bergeragreed that domestic automaking needs an urgent "reset," but predicted that Germany could still "preserve a sustainably profitable core of automotive value creation.".

In other words, car making in Germany may shrink, but what remains could be leaner, more specialized and more profitable.

Sources indicate that many doomsayers overlook the fact that Mercedes' investment halt is tied to tough negotiations with unions over cutting labor costs at its German plants. This includes scrapping the 35-hour workweek. The investment freeze could be lifted if a deal is reached.

Even so, Achim Kampker, an electric mobility engineering professor at RWTH Aachen University, sees the investment cuts as more than a negotiating tactic.

Kampker compared China's lightning-fast industrial strategy with Germany's, which he remarked was "too slow," as excessive bureaucracy and complex business structures prevent value creation.

"We need to become faster, more innovative and significantly more productive," Kampker told DW.

Recent findings suggest that china's EV-makers can bring a fresh model to market in around 20 months, versus 48 to 60 months for Germany, according to Roland Berger. Plus, the Chinese have a 30% cost advantage.

Production costs at German plants are also much higher — between €3,500 ($3,840) and €5,000 per vehicle — than in Eastern Europe, where they range from €2,000 to €2,500.

A separate report by consultancy PwC in September noted that despite German carmakers being well managed, well capitalized and knowing exactly what is coming, they may have a "false sense of security.".

PwC remarked Germany needs to focus on four areas to ensure its auto industry is "future-fit" to compete with China.

These include splitting its internal combustion engine (ICE) business from the electric vehicle (EV) business, investing bumper ICE profits into those new technologies, redesigning workplace culture and training, and leveraging existing partnerships with Chinese automakers and US tech firms.

"The future viability of the German automotive industry depends significantly on decisions made in the next 12 to 18 months," wrote Harald Wimmer, global and German automotive leader at PwC Germany.

With the transition to EVs, some predict that automaking will become part of a much larger global electronics sector, which Germany must exploit.

Wimmer noted how top Chinese automakers were already benchmarking themselves against consumer electronics giants. These include smartphone maker Xiaomi, which now also produces around 400,000 EVs per year.

"Anyone who continues to base their competitive framework solely on their own industry is making a mistake that cannot be corrected once it becomes apparent," he warned.

Despite all the doom and gloom, car production within Germany is holding up pretty well.

Domestic manufacturing sits around 12% lower than pre-pandemic levels. This year, however, the auto sector is on course to meet a December estimate of 4.11 million vehicles, just 1% lower than last year, according to the German Association of the Automotive Industry (VDA).

IW Köln's Puls thinks German automakers must now avoid a trap Italy fell into in the early 2000s when its national auto champion, Fiat, struggled with profitability.

Sources indicate that in Italy, "the politics and the unions blocked any attempt by Fiat to cut overcapacity," Puls told DW. "What's the result? They have a capacity of 1.1 to 1.2 million cars and utilization of about 250,000.".

Last year, those same Italian plants built just 214,000 passenger cars, according to the FIM Cisl trade union, the fewest since 1954.

For Germany, the glitch isn't a lack of expertise or ambition; it's that reforms to huge industries often get weighed down by caution and red tape.

As the country's auto giants try to push through painful cuts, RWTH Aachen University's Kampker warned that if they fail to address their shortcomings, "we will see more production sites closing and a substantial shift of industrial investment and employment away from Germany.".

"There is still an opportunity to reverse this trend, but the window of opportunity is narrowing," Kampker concluded.
