Germany's religious freedom report: Authoritarian regimes, holy wars, and spies abroad

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1181 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that the report spans more than 150 pages, but its conclusion can be summed up in a single sentence: "The global situation regarding freedom of religion and belief deteriorated during the reporting period," stated Thomas Rachel, the German government's commissioner for freedom of religion and belief, and a member of parliament for the center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU).
  • Industry observers note that the government has issued a dedicated report on freedom of religion and belief around the world.
  • To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the report spans more than 150 pages, but its conclusion can be summed up in a single sentence: "The global situation regarding freedom of religion and belief deteriorated during the reporting period," stated Thomas Rachel, the German government's commissioner for freedom of religion and belief, and a member of parliament for the center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU). Recently adopted by the Cabinet, the government's fourth report on the subject covers developments from 2023 to 2025.

Industry observers note that the government has issued a dedicated report on freedom of religion and belief around the world. According to the report, this freedom is facing "increasing pressure" globally. The focus is not primarily on the suppression of religious institutions or structures, but on the situation of individuals who hold a religious belief, or none at all.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

It has been revealed that the importance of religious freedom is reflected in the way the government commissioner describes the issue: "Religion and faith are of great importance to four out of five people around the world and are central to their identity. People wake up with God and go to sleep with God. It is part of their everyday lives." Research by the Pew Research Center suggests that about 84% of the world's population identifies with a certain religion.

Recent findings suggest that at a time when authoritarian regimes are gaining ground and expanding their surveillance capabilities, the report paints a bleak picture. The growing number of violent conflicts, the rise of authoritarian rule, and the spread of populism have led to "painful restrictions on freedom of religion and belief around the world.".

The German government report does not attempt to provide a statistical tally of attacks or the number of people facing persecution. Instead, it examines 30 countries as case studies where, in the federal government's view, freedom of religion and belief is being restricted. These include about six countries each from Africa, Asia, and the Arab world. In Europe, the report focuses on Belarus, Russia, Ukraine, and Turkey, while in Latin America it highlights Mexico, Nicaragua, and Cuba. It also identifies shortcomings in five of the world's six most populous countries: China, India, Indonesia, Pakistan, and Nigeria.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Sources indicate that regarding India, the report refers to "Hindu nationalist efforts" that threaten the equal treatment of all officially recognized religions. It states that the generally peaceful coexistence of different faiths is "repeatedly overshadowed by tensions and, at times, violence." Both Muslim and Christian communities report growing intolerance and hate speech. According to the report, violent Hindu extremist groups have carried out a "large number of physical attacks" against Muslims, while the police and government authorities often respond inadequately.

In China, the German government identifies a "significant tightening of the legal framework of state control at the expense of freedom of religion and belief." According to the report, this particularly affects Uyghurs, Tibetans and churches that lack official state approval and are subject to harsh measures by the authorities. The law on the "Promotion of Ethnic Unity and Progress," which came into force on July 1, 2026, subordinates religion to "the formation of national identity" and patriotic education.

One of the countries where the situation has deteriorated most dramatically is Nicaragua, which has severely restricted freedom of religion and belief since 2018. The repression has primarily targeted the Catholic Church. According to the report, "intimidation, persecution, imprisonment, and expulsion" have forced around 130 priests and nuns to leave the country.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Sources indicate that the reports reserves some of its sharpest criticism for Kirill, the patriarch of the Russian Orthodox Church. Under his leadership, the church has strongly supported Russia's war against Ukraine and portrayed it as a "holy war." According to the report, "weapons are blessed, Russian soldiers are absolved of their sins, and donations are collected for the war." It is perhaps the clearest example in the report of how religion can be used to justify oppression and violence.

The report explicitly addresses the threat posed by "transnational repression" (TNR), which it describes as a "growing global problem" that also affects Germany. The term refers to the persecution or intimidation of individuals by their country of origin beyond its own borders.

Ultimately, it argues, this amounts to a "continuation of domestic repression." Such "cross-border repression" has become considerably easier through the growing availability of digital means of repression, including smear campaigns on social media and spyware.

Sources indicate that these forms of pressure range from physical attacks on individuals to digital assaults such as online intimidation and defamation. In some cases, repression is also carried out by threatening family members who remain in the country of origin. Russia and Iran, for example, are identified as the "main perpetrators of transnational repression" in Germany.

China is a particularly prominent example of religious and ideological tensions. Repression by Beijing in Germany primarily targets members of groups that the country's Communist Party classifies as "hostile to the system." These include Uyghurs, Tibetans, and members of the Falun Gong movement. According to the report, they are "also subject to surveillance and repressive measures in Germany," while relatives living in China are pressured.

Thomas Rachel hopes the newly published report will be "discussed in as many Bundestag committees as possible" and that members of parliament will "engage with the concern accordingly." Previous government reports on the subject have been debated in the Bundestag plenary at least once and, in some cases, twice.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Recent findings suggest that the issue's place within the German government has also changed during the current legislative term. Commissioner Thomas Rachel is now based at the Foreign Ministry, while both of his predecessors since 2018 were attached to the Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development. Today, Rachel says, the importance of religion is being "taken into account" in German foreign policy. He also points to his involvement in the Foreign Ministry's diplomatic training programs.

In doing so, the government led by Chancellor Friedrich Merz (CDU) reversed a structural decision made by the previous center-left coalition, which was led from 2021 to 2025 by Chancellor Olaf Scholz of the Social Democratic Party (SPD). The Scholz government had reduced the issue's prominence by assigning it to the "Religion and Foreign Policy" division. Religion and foreign policy have now regained a more prominent place within government.

One example is the current foreign minister, Johann Wadephul, who has already visited the Vatican more often than his two predecessors combined. In addition, alongside Rachel, the ministry has for some time maintained a dedicated unit headed by an ambassador that deals with, among other things, "fundamental complications relating to religion and foreign policy.".

Kwame Brathwaite, photographer of 'Black is Beautiful' movement, dies at 85

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Editor’s Note:  This article was originally published by The Art Newspaper, an editorial partner of CNN Style.
  • Kwame Brathwaite, the pioneering activist and photographer whose work helped define the aesthetics of the “Black is Beautiful” movement of the 1960s and beyond, died on April 1, aged 85.
  • His son, Kwame Brathwaite, Jr, unveiled his father’s death in an Instagram post that read in part, “I am deeply saddened to share that my Baba, the patriarch of our family, our rock and my hero has transitioned.”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Editor’s Note:  This article was originally published by The Art Newspaper, an editorial partner of CNN Style.

Kwame Brathwaite, the pioneering activist and photographer whose work helped define the aesthetics of the “Black is Beautiful” movement of the 1960s and beyond, died on April 1, aged 85.

His son, Kwame Brathwaite, Jr, unveiled his father’s death in an Instagram post that read in part, “I am deeply saddened to share that my Baba, the patriarch of our family, our rock and my hero has transitioned.”.

Brathwaite’s work has been the subject of resurgent interest from curators, historians and collectors in recent years, and his first major institutional retrospective, which was organized by the Aperture Foundation, made its debut in 2019 at the Skirball Cultural Center in Los Angeles before touring the country.

Brathwaite was born in 1938 to Barbadian immigrants, in what he referred to as “the People’s Republic of Brooklyn” in New York, though his family moved from there to Harlem and then to the South Bronx when Brathwaite was 5 years old. He attended the School of Industrial Art (now the High School of Art and Design) and, according to profiles of Brathwaite in T Magazine and Vice, was drawn to photography by two moments. The first was in August of 1955, when a 17-year-old Brathwaite encountered David Jackson’s haunting photograph of a brutalized Emmett Till in his open casket. The second was in 1956, when — after he and his brother Elombe co-founded the African Jazz Arts Society and Studios (AJASS) — Brathwaite saw a young man taking photos in a dark jazz club without the use of a flash, and his mind became alight with possibility.

Using a Hasselblad medium-format camera, Brathwaite attempted to do the same, learning to work with limited light in a manner that enhanced the visual narrative of his imagery. He would soon also develop a darkroom technique that enriched and deepened how Black skin would appear in his photography, honing the practice in a small darkroom in his Harlem apartment. Brathwaite went on to photograph jazz legends performing throughout the 1950s and ’60s, including Miles Davis, John Coltrane, Thelonious Monk and others.

It has been revealed that “You want to get the feeling, the mood that you’re experiencing when they’re playing,” Brathwaite told Aperture Magazine in 2017. “That’s the thing. You want to capture that.”.

A 106-year-old from the Philippines is Vogue's oldest ever cover model.

By the early 1960s, alongside the rest of AJASS, Brathwaite began using his photography and organizing prowess to consciously push back against whitewashed, Eurocentric beauty standards. The group came up with the concept of the Grandassa Models, young Black women whom Brathwaite would photograph, celebrating and accentuating their features. In 1962, AJASS organized “Naturally ’62”, a fashion show held in a Harlem club called the Purple Manor and featuring the models. The show would go on to be held regularly until 1992. In 1966, Brathwaite married his wife Sikolo, a Grandassa Model whom he had met on the street the year prior when he asked if he could take her portrait. The two remained married for the rest of Brathwaite’s life.

Industry observers note that by the 1970s, Brathwaite’s focus on jazz shifted to other forms of popular Black music. In 1974, he traveled to Africa with the Jackson Five to document their tour, also photographing the historic “Rumble in the Jungle” boxing match between Muhammad Ali and George Foreman in what’s now the Democratic Republic of Congo that same year. Commissions in this era also saw Brathwaite photographing Nina Simone, Stevie Wonder, Sly and the Family Stone, Bob Marley and other music legends.

Creating for community: The Black designers placing identity and heritage at the center of their brands.

Throughout the ensuing decades, Brathwaite continued to explore and develop his mode of photography, all through the lens of the “Black is Beautiful” ethos. In 2016, Brathwaite joined the roster of Philip Martin Gallery in Los Angeles, and he was continuing to photograph commissions as recently as 2018, when he shot artist and stylist Joanne Petit-Frère for The New Yorker.

In a recent development, T Magazine’s 2021 profile, published on the occasion of Brathwaite’s retrospective traveling to the Blanton Museum of Art in Austin, Texas, noted that the photographer’s health was failing such that he was unable to be interviewed for the article. A separate exhibition, “Kwame Brathwaite: Things Well Worth Waiting For,” is currently on view at the Art Institute of Chicago, where it will remain until July 24.

Top image: Kwame Brathwaite, “Untitled (Sikolo Brathwaite, Orange Portrait),” 1968.

Sources indicate that before we dive into what makes this Galaxy Projector Night Light so great, there are a couple of pressing issues to address. No variant of this USB-powered star projector will break up heated dinner arguments by casting a beautifully animated space whale on the ceiling, as one ridiculous AI-generated advert asserts. Its projections are eye-catching enough to entertain space fans young and old, but they’re strictly static.

Also, while you might be tempted by the lure of 24 interchangeable slides, compared to this Galaxy Projector Night Light’s 13, this lesser model’s slide selection is a letdown. As much as I enjoy Christmas, if I had Santa’s colossal face gazing down at me from the ceiling I’d never sleep again.

I tempered my expectations when I first got my hands on the Galaxy Projector Night Light. Packed in a small, relatively unassuming box, it looks remarkably similar to the standard model that’s spread across TikTok, YouTube, Facebook and so on. Just like that one, it’s powered via USB, with a flexible stalk, a slot for slides and a nose-mounted focus wheel.

In a recent development, however, once I hooked it up to a handy USB socket, all my reservations vanished, and I was seriously impressed by the power of this little projector. You’ll need a darkened room but the Galaxy Projector Night Light’s larger lens is a serious step-up from the run-of-the-mill version. Its images are richer and clearer than you’d expect from a projector this size, and easily capable of transforming a mid-sized ceiling or wall into a cosmic display.

This stunning James Webb Space Telescope image of the Pillars of Creation, with its vast columns of gas and dust, is a perfect example of the projections on offer. The fact the display was static didn’t diminish its wow factor, and I spent a good 15 minutes gazing at it in wonder.

The Galaxy Projector Night Light does have a four-hour shut-off in case you drift off or want to use it to lull a child to sleep (and 12 hours for its night light function). It’s easy to adjust thanks to its flexible neck, and while it never once came loose, you’ll find some USB ports have a tighter grip than others.

Once I set aside the images of Santa Claus (you’re staying in the box, Saint Nick), jellyfish and a T. rex, I was left with 10 astronomy-related slides. Several, such as the black hole, are artistic illustrations, while others, like the aforementioned Pillars, are actual astronomical images.

According to recent reports, they all have their own distinct appeal. I wouldn’t, for example, describe the black hole slide as relaxing, but it’s absolutely captivating in a cosmic horror way. I’d have appreciated an auto-rotate option, but that would have added some bulk to the projector.

Sources indicate that switching slides is a breeze, each image mounted in its own slide holder. Oddly, a couple of mine had hair-like marks, but those disappeared when I brought the image into focus via the nose wheel.

Industry observers note that the Galaxy Projector Night Light will run off any USB port: a laptop, desktop, charger and so on. Some of the best star projectors are styled so they blend in with a room, but this one is so small you can just pack it away until you need it. As long as you don’t buy the hype and think you’re getting something that’ll bathe a room in beautifully animated starscapes, as several Amazon purchasers did, you’ll find this Galaxy Projector Night Light is a surprisingly capable little star projector.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A discovery by chemists at Brown University is challenging a basic principle of chemical bonding that has appeared in textbooks for generations. The researchers have found direct experimental evidence that triple bonds involving heavy elements do not always behave according to the familiar rules taught in chemistry classes.

The study, published in the journal Science, reveals that Einstein's theory of relativity can fundamentally alter the structure of chemical bonds when atoms become sufficiently heavy. In particular, the researchers found that two types of bonds normally treated as distinct can begin to merge, creating a structure that conventional chemistry models do not fully describe.

Using a powerful analytical technique called photoelectron spectroscopy, the Brown team identified the unmistakable signature of these relativistic effects in bonds formed between carbon and bismuth, a heavy metallic element.

According to recent reports, "This idea that relativity is vital in heavy elements has been around since the 1970s," stated Lai-Sheng Wang, a professor of chemistry at Brown and the study's corresponding author. "But we show direct spectroscopic evidence that what we learned in high school about chemical bonding isn't true in heavy elements.".

Why Einstein's Relativity Changes Chemical Bonds.

To understand why the discovery matters, it helps to look at how chemical bonds normally form.

Atoms can connect by sharing electrons, the negatively charged particles that surround their positively charged nuclei. In a simple covalent bond, each atom contributes an electron to a shared pair. The attraction between these negatively charged electrons and the two positive nuclei helps hold the atoms together.

Industry observers note that some atoms share multiple pairs of electrons, producing double or triple bonds. According to the standard textbook model, a triple bond consists of three separate connections: one sigma bond and two pi bonds.

According to recent reports, the sigma bond is typically the strongest. It forms through a direct, "head-on" overlap of electron orbitals along the axis connecting the two atomic nuclei. The other two connections are pi bonds, which form through weaker, "side-by-side" overlaps on either side of that axis.

For lighter elements, this familiar description works well. However, the situation becomes more complicated farther down the periodic table.

It has been revealed that heavy elements contain nuclei with large numbers of protons, creating powerful electrical attractions that can accelerate nearby electrons to a substantial fraction of the speed of light. At these extreme speeds, effects predicted by Einstein's theory of relativity become vital, changing how the electrons behave.

Sources indicate that one particularly notable effect is known as spin-orbit coupling. Electrons possess a quantum property called spin, which gives them a magnetic character often described as pointing up or down. Under ordinary conditions, spin and orbital motion can be treated as largely separate properties. But in heavy atoms, relativistic effects can link them strongly together.

That connection changes how electrons interact and disrupts the clear distinction between sigma and pi bonds that traditional chemistry relies on.

Recent findings suggest that "The boundary between a sigma bond and a pi bond is now sort of smeared," Wang said. "We still have three bonds, but we don't really strictly have a sigma or a pi anymore.".

Scientists Find Direct Evidence in Bismuth Bonds.

To test whether this unusual bonding behavior actually occurs, Wang's research group, led by Brown Ph.D. students Deniz Kahraman and Jie Hui, created molecules containing carbon and bismuth.

Bismuth sits next to lead on the periodic table and is among the heavier elements in which relativistic effects are expected to play a major role. That made it an especially useful candidate for investigating whether the familiar rules of triple bonding begin to break down.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers cooled the molecules to temperatures approaching absolute zero, the lowest temperature theoretically possible. They then examined the molecules using photoelectron spectroscopy, a technique that uses laser light to eject electrons from molecules.

According to recent reports, by measuring the energy of the released electrons, scientists can determine how tightly those electrons were held in place. This provides a detailed picture of the electronic structure responsible for chemical bonding.

The results revealed a striking departure from the conventional model.

Rather than showing the expected combination of one sigma bond and two pi bonds, the carbon-bismuth triple bonds displayed a different arrangement. Their electronic structure was more consistent with one pi bond and two hybrid sigma-pi bonds.

In other words, Einstein's relativity had changed the nature of the chemical connections, blending two traditionally distinct types of bonds into something that standard textbook descriptions do not fully capture.

A Discovery That Could Rewrite Chemistry Textbooks.

The findings provide direct experimental confirmation of relativistic bonding effects that scientists have discussed for decades. Wang believes this evidence could eventually lead to changes in how chemical bonding is explained in chemistry textbooks, particularly as research involving heavy elements continues to expand.

The implications could also extend beyond fundamental chemistry.

Bismuth has attracted growing scientific interest because it may offer a less toxic alternative to lead in next-generation solar cells. Researchers are also exploring its potential in quantum materials and quantum computing, fields that depend on understanding and controlling the behavior of electrons.

A more accurate picture of how heavy atoms form chemical bonds could help scientists investigate these materials and better understand the properties that make them useful for emerging technologies.

"Maybe this will become the new textbook idea as we are dealing with more and more heavy chemistry of the heavy elements," Wang said.

The research was supported by the U.S. National Science Foundation (CHE-2403841) and the U.S. Department of Energy (DE-SC0008501).

Study finds slightly higher risk of autism diagnosis in areas with more lithium in drinking water, but experts say more research is needed

📅 03 Apr 2023 | ⏱️ 5 min read (975 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNN

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A newly introduced study found a moderately higher risk of autism spectrum disorder in children born to pregnant people exposed to tap water with higher levels of lithium, but experts caution that this association does not show a direct link between the two.
  • About 1 in 36 children in the US is diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) each year, according to data from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
  • Sources indicate that scientists still don’t know the exact cause of autism, a developmental disorder.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A newly introduced study found a moderately higher risk of autism spectrum disorder in children born to pregnant people exposed to tap water with higher levels of lithium, but experts caution that this association does not show a direct link between the two.

About 1 in 36 children in the US is diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) each year, according to data from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

Sources indicate that scientists still don’t know the exact cause of autism, a developmental disorder. Genetics may be a factor, but some have been looking at potential environmental causes, too.

Autism diagnosis has become more common, but pandemic disrupted early detection, CDC says.

Sources indicate that cases may be on the rise, but that is also unclear. One study published this year on cases in the New York-New Jersey area found that autism diagnosis rates tripled among certain age groups between 2000 and 2016. A 2021 report found similar increases in cases, but the CDC claims the increased number of cases is most likely linked to more doctors screening for the condition.

Recent findings suggest that lithium is an alkali metal that can be found naturally in some food and ground water. It’s used in batteries, grease and air conditioners, as well as in the treatment of bipolar disorder and some blood disorders. Its levels in US drinking water are not regulated, according to the US Geological Survey.

A newly introduced study, published Monday in the journal JAMA Pediatrics, found a small association between lithium and autism diagnosis in Denmark, where the researchers say the level of lithium in drinking water is similar to that in American water systems.

The researchers checked a database of people with psychiatric disorders for children born between 2000 and 2013 to find information on 8,842 cases of ASD and 43,864 participants who did not have ASD. They then measured the concentration of lithium in 151 public waterworks that served more than half of the Danish population and mapped out where pregnant people lived in relation.

For many neurodiverse people, 'The Sims' has been a lifelong comfort.

As lithium levels in water increased, there was a modest increased risk of an ASD diagnosis. Specifically, compared with people at the lowest exposure level, those who had the second and third highest exposure during pregnancy had a 24% to 26% higher risk of ASD diagnosed in children. The group with the highest exposure had a 46% higher risk than those at the lowest level of exposure.

The researchers could not tell how much water the pregnant people drank, but they picked Denmark in part because residents there consume some of the lowest amounts of bottled water in Europe.

Experts say it’s important to note that the research can’t show that lithium exposure leads directly to an autism diagnosis.

Industry observers note that further study is required, stated study co-author Dr. Beate Ritz, a professor of neurology in the David Geffen School of Medicine at UCLA, and a professor of epidemiology and environmental health at the UCLA Fielding School of Public Health.

“Any drinking water contaminants that may affect the developing human brain deserve intense scrutiny,” Ritz mentioned in a news release. She added that the research would need to be replicated in other countries to look for a similar connection.

The implications of the findings are complex as far as public health policy is concerned, according to an editorial published alongside the study. Lithium levels in water, at concentrations that the study associated with a potential ASD risk, have also been linked with health benefits such as lower rates of hospitalization for psychiatric disorders and suicide.

Sources indicate that “If all these of associations are valid, the wisdom of Solomon will be required to develop guidelines for lithium in drinking water that are maximally protective of the entire population,” wrote Dr. David C. Bellinger, a professor of neurology and psychology at Harvard Medical School. “Until the basic biology of ASD is better understood, it will be difficult to distinguish causal from spurious associations.”.

'Heartbreaking' delays in autism diagnosis and treatment got even worse during pandemic.

Dr. Max Wiznitzer, director of the Rainbow Autism Center at University Hospitals Rainbow Babies and Children’s Hospital in Cleveland, points to other research on the effects of lithium on pregnant people who take it for mental health disorders. Those studies – which look at people exposed to much higher levels than are found in drinking water – do not show a connection with autism spectrum disorder.

“It’s an interesting association, but causation is definitely not proven,” said Wiznitzer, who was not involved in the upcoming research. “We have to see if there’s a viable and biologically plausible mechanism by which a small amount of lithium in the water supply can somehow do this, yet pharmacologic dosing of lithium in women with bipolar disorder has not been reported to be causing increased risk of ASD.”.

Other studies have also suggested connections between ASD and environmental exposures to things like pesticides, air pollution and phthalates. But none of them points to any of these factors as a direct cause of the disorder.

A link between environmental exposure and ASD is hard to prove, Wiznitzer said. With research showing that increased exposure to air pollution raises the risk of giving birth to a child with ASD, for example, he often wonders whether pollution is the determining factor or if it’s just the populations who live in more polluted areas.

“There’s a lot of speculation about about environmental factors, but how many of them are truly causally associated?” Wiznitzer noted. “We are bombarded with a variety of environmental stressors in our everyday lives. We have to figure out how to basically safely navigate them, and this is probably not one that’s high on our list.”.

Breaking: A mysterious gap hints at black holes born from stars that never exploded

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1118 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, the biggest stars in the universe often end their lives in spectacular explosions called supernovae, hurling enormous amounts of material into space.
  • In a recent development, new research led by Caltech has uncovered intriguing evidence that this quieter form of stellar death may help explain the origins of many black holes.
  • Industry observers note that the discoveries build on a decade of gravitational wave astronomy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the biggest stars in the universe often end their lives in spectacular explosions called supernovae, hurling enormous amounts of material into space. Their remaining cores collapse under gravity, forming neutron stars or, in some cases, black holes. But scientists have long suspected that some massive stars meet a very different fate. Instead of exploding, they may collapse directly into neutron stars or black holes, effectively disappearing without a bang.

In a recent development, new research led by Caltech has uncovered intriguing evidence that this quieter form of stellar death may help explain the origins of many black holes. Using gravitational wave observations from the LIGO, Virgo, and KAGRA detector network, researchers identified patterns suggesting that a distinct population of black holes could have formed from stars that never went supernova. Although the findings do not directly confirm the existence of these failed supernovae, they closely match theoretical predictions about how such black holes should be distributed.

Industry observers note that the discoveries build on a decade of gravitational wave astronomy. LIGO, the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-wave Observatory, is funded by the National Science Foundation (NSF) and operates detectors in Louisiana and Washington. In 2015, the observatory made history by directly detecting gravitational waves for the first time. These tiny disturbances in spacetime were generated by two black holes colliding. Since then, LIGO has teamed up with the Virgo observatory in Italy and the Kamioka Gravitational-wave Detector (KAGRA) in Japan. Together, the network has recorded more than 300 black hole collisions.

A Hidden Population of Black Holes.

"A vast majority of the merging black holes in the universe are about 10 times the mass of our Sun," says LIGO team member Katerina Chatziioannou, a Caltech physics professor and William H. Hurt Scholar. "Our data are showing that this group of black holes may have a common origin -- they may be a distinct subpopulation that failed to go supernova. These results represent a connection between the gravitational-wave data and underlying astrophysics we are trying to extract.".

Recent findings suggest that chatziioannou led the study, which was published in Physical Review D. The lead author, Isaac Legred (PhD '25), is now a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign and completed the work while at Caltech. Jacob Golomb (PhD '25), a former member of Chatziioannou's research group who now works at Asari AI, also contributed to the research.

Despite decades of investigation, astronomers have yet to confirm a specific case of a failed supernova. The theory, however, has a strong scientific foundation. Researchers have proposed that many merging black holes weighing approximately 10 times as much as the Sun may have originated from stars that collapsed without exploding. In these mergers, either the heavier black hole or both black holes could have formed through this process. The Caltech team set out to determine whether existing gravitational wave observations supported that possibility.

A Mysterious Gap in Black Hole Masses.

Recent findings suggest that to investigate, the scientists examined the masses of black holes involved in 257 mergers detected by the LIGO, Virgo, and KAGRA network during the past decade. A striking pattern emerged. Black holes weighing roughly 10 times the mass of the Sun were exceptionally common, appearing in about three-quarters of the merger sample.

Even more surprisingly, the researchers identified a noticeable shortage of black holes weighing between 12 and 16 solar masses. This was the first time such a distinct gap had been found in the mass distribution, raising new questions about what determines the sizes of black holes when they form.

Sources indicate that "We see 10 solar-mass black holes merging all the time," Legred indicates. "But why are, say, 14 solar-mass black holes so rare? The gap we see in the distribution of masses indicates there may be a special cocktail of internal physics that goes into forming the abundance of 10 solar-mass black holes.".

Recent findings suggest that the researchers also examined how rapidly the black holes rotate, since their spin rates can preserve clues about the conditions under which they formed. They found that black holes near 10 solar masses tended to have spin rates concentrated within a smaller range than those of the broader black hole population (the spins are also influenced by how the black holes formed).

Taken together, the unusual concentration of black hole masses, the scarcity of objects in the 12 to 16 solar mass range, and the similarities in their rotation suggest that these black holes may belong to a distinct population with a shared formation history. One possible explanation is that many originated when massive stars collapsed directly into black holes without producing supernova explosions.

Gravitational Waves Offer Clues to Silent Stellar Deaths.

Finding stars that disappear without exploding presents a major challenge for astronomers. Ordinary supernovae produce brilliant flashes that can be detected across enormous cosmic distances. Failed supernovae, by contrast, may leave little visible evidence of what happened, making it difficult to identify them through conventional observations.

According to recent reports, "We can look up at the sky and try to study historical records of massive stars that failed to explode, but it's challenging because they just vanish without exploding, leaving a dark patch of sky," Legred says. "With this study, we show the gravitational-wave data are consistent with most binary black holes forming from a very special kind of failed supernova, but more research is needed. Black holes are born in some of the most extreme environments in the universe, so the prospect of better understanding their formation is very exciting.".

By studying the gravitational waves released when black holes merge, scientists can investigate the origins of objects whose formation may have produced little or no visible explosion. The new findings provide another piece of evidence that massive stars can follow different paths at the ends of their lives, potentially revealing how a substantial fraction of the universe's black holes came into existence.

Recent findings suggest that the research, titled "Low-mass failed supernovae and the 10 solar-mass peak in the merging black hole mass distribution," received funding from the National Science Foundation, the U.S. Department of Energy, and the Simons Foundation. LIGO is operated by Caltech and MIT.

U.S. officially loses measles elimination status amid ongoing outbreaks

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • on Tuesday lost its official designation as a measles-free nation, more than 25 years after it eliminated the highly contagious virus.
  • Sources indicate that the Pan American Health Organization announced the decision, which came after an independent panel of eight scientific experts convened last week to consider the country's epidemiological evidence.
  • In other words, measles is spreading regularly in the country again, with ongoing outbreaks sparking new ones.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the U.S. on Tuesday lost its official designation as a measles-free nation, more than 25 years after it eliminated the highly contagious virus.

Sources indicate that the Pan American Health Organization announced the decision, which came after an independent panel of eight scientific experts convened last week to consider the country's epidemiological evidence. The director of PAHO, the regional branch of the World Health Organization, made the final call that measles is endemic — or always present — in the U.S. following 12 months of continuous transmission.

In other words, measles is spreading regularly in the country again, with ongoing outbreaks sparking new ones.

"The commission concluded that endemic measles transmission has now been reestablished in Bolivia, Mexico and the United States, and recommended that their measles elimination status be withdrawn — a recommendation which I have accepted," Dr. Jarbas Barbosa, PAHO director, noted during a news briefing on Tuesday.

Sources indicate that it's a devastating step backward for American public health, as declining childhood vaccination rates and vaccine hesitancy fuel outbreaks across the country that have sickened thousands of people and led to a tragic string of preventable deaths. Among the deaths where vaccination status was reported, all were unvaccinated.

More than 5,400 measles cases had been reported nationwide in 2026 as of mid-November, marking the country's worst outbreak in more than three decades. States have confirmed 10 deaths associated with the disease so far in 2026: seven in Pennsylvania, one in Upcoming York and two in Wisconsin.

According to recent reports, the commission found that out of 52 U.S. states and territories it tracked, 48 experienced measles outbreaks during the reporting period between January 2025 and January 2026, PAHO Assistant Director Dr. Rhonda Sealey-Thomas noted during the briefing. But Barbosa said the countries are already taking action to control outbreaks, such as strengthening vaccination, surveillance for timely case detection and outbreak response efforts.

Recent findings suggest that the U.S. in particular has ramped up vaccination efforts to close immunity gaps, particularly in areas with low immunization coverage experiencing outbreaks, stated Dr. Daniel Salas, executive manager of PAHO's Special Program for Comprehensive Immunization. He said PAHO expects the U.S. to present its corrective action strategy in the coming weeks, outlining strategies to regain its designation.

In a Tuesday release, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said it will continue to ensure all communities have the resources to prevent and respond to outbreaks and is committed to working with states and other local partners to restore the U.S.'s measles elimination status.

Recent findings suggest that CDC Director Dr. Erica Schwartz noted in the release that the measles elimination designation "is not what protects Americans. Vaccination does." She said the agency has invested $100 million in state and local health departments to reach communities where transmission is occurring.

Last week, Schwartz told Reuters that the agency is going to be "doing the same exact thing that we've been doing today" if the U.S. loses its measles-free status.

Sources indicate that the decision also poses a newly introduced test for the Trump administration and its Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who has taken steps to change recommendations for the childhood measles, mumps and rubella, or MMR, vaccine and has a long history of questioning its safety without evidence.

But Kennedy, in a Tuesday X post, stated he continues to recommend MMR vaccination as "the most effective way to prevent measles.".

Sources indicate that "We are working to close vaccination gaps and rebuild public trust," Kennedy said. "We will answer families' questions honestly about vaccine benefits and risks and work with trusted health care providers and community leaders to prevent measles, limit its spread, and support timely treatment.".

Sources indicate that CNBC previously reported on how the return of measles in the U.S. exposes weaknesses in the nation's public health system that raise concerns about the return of other eliminated diseases. The resurgence of measles exposes eroding trust in health institutions and growing challenges in persuading people to protect themselves, their children and their communities.

Public health experts previously told CNBC that the return of measles ultimately boils down to fewer children getting vaccinated.

It has been revealed that the MMR vaccine is about 97% effective against measles after two doses, while a single dose is 93% effective, according to the CDC. Yet data aggregated by the CDC demonstrates that vaccination coverage for that shot among U.S. kindergarteners fell to 92.4% in the 2025-2026 school year, which is below the 95% threshold public health officials generally recommend to prevent sustained transmission.

The American Medical Association urged the public to get vaccinated after PAHO's announcement.

According to recent reports, "We must treat the current measles outbreaks as an urgent call to rebuild trust in science-based recommendations and restore strong, fully-funded public health infrastructure to protect families and communities and prevent the return of diseases once eliminated," AMA President Dr. Willie Underwood noted in a statement.

In a separate statement, the pharmaceutical industry's largest lobbying group called on policymakers to provide "clear, accurate information about the seriousness of measles infection and the effectiveness of vaccines against it, restore and sustain high vaccination coverage in every community, strengthen vaccination efforts, and invest in disease surveillance and rapid outbreak response.".

"We have the tools to eliminate measles again and what we need now is the commitment to use them," said Dr. Michael Ybarra, chief medical officer of the Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America.

Measles isn't just a public health threat — it's also a huge financial burden on the healthcare system, CNBC reported.

Based on this year's case count, a fresh tool developed by researchers at Johns Hopkins University estimates an economic cost of nearly $83 million for the outbreaks. That total includes $56 million in public health response costs, almost $25 million in lost productivity and more than $1.8 million in direct medical expenses.

In a recent development, the U.S. now joins Canada, Spain and the U.K., which all recently lost their measles-free status after a review by experts at the World Health Organization. While the U.S. dropped out of the WHO, it remains a member of PAHO, its Americas branch.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On a sweltering July morning, in the middle of an empty playground in suburban Denver, two extremely fit, sweaty, shirtless male influencers are tussling in the dirt.

In a recent development, “The guy on top who’s in control, we call that position riding,” one of the grapplers, Carlos Monteon Jr. pauses to explain to a group of eight similarly fit, sweaty, nearly all shirtless men who are watching the action in a circle. Monteon is a wrestler and influencer from Arizona, with pomelo-sized biceps, glossy shoulder-length hair, and more than 675,000 followers across TikTok and Instagram. He turns to his demo partner, Johnny Cole, a rangy, then 28-year-old content creator (59,000 TikTok followers) with a penchant for slutty tank tops. “And this one is called the Saturday night ride.”.

It has been revealed that monteon and Cole continue scuffling. The match ends with Monteon straddling Cole, their faces inches apart, their torsos glistening. The scene looks like a JV wrestling match.

The other men pair up to take turns grappling. Two cameramen circle them as a drone hums overhead.

“Yes, testosterone!” one influencer yells.

According to recent reports, “And estrogen!” Cole adds. “Both of them together, as one!”.

According to recent reports, I’m at Hey Brother House, a content incubator that hosts weeklong retreats for male social media influencers. The organization teaches men and boys “to embody healthy masculinity, fully process emotions, embrace authenticity, and show up as compassionate, empathetic community leaders,” according to its website.

Filmmaker Vince Nett captures the shirtless shenanigans of Carlos Monteon Jr.

Sources indicate that cole, the founder of Hey Brother, helms the project with two other house leaders. Jonathan Jacobs, an affable 37-year-old who owns a digital marketing agency in Los Angeles, is wearing a brown cap that states “Male Friendship.” Matthew Echelman, a 35-year-old Brooklyn-based filmmaker, has hired two crew members to film the whole thing for a possible future documentary. Funded by a grant of more than $180,000 from an initiative called the Young Men and Media Collective, Hey Brother House’s goal is to flood 18-to-25-year-old men’s social media feeds with content that will (hopefully) make them less terrible.

Industry observers note that the house itself is a rented stucco McMansion next to the Green Valley Ranch Golf Club, a residential community just outside Denver. In some respects, it looks like your average fratty domicile: There’s a Nintendo Switch console in the living room, where the boys play Mario Kart; a basement decked out with fitness equipment, a sauna, air hockey, and Foosball; and a makeshift indoor putting green. But there’s also a strict house alcohol ban, remote-controlled bidets, a box of wigs, swag boxes filled with fuchsia “Redefining Masculinity” T-shirts, and a wall covered in Post-Its of “gifts” the men can give each other, including “laying down on couch or blanket in park with my head on your lap.” There’s even a room—the “Man Box”—for testimonials, where the “cast members” can speak directly to the camera about their day. It’s reminiscent of reality TV, except most everyone is aware of bell hooks’ All About Love: Newly introduced Visions, and they are explicitly here to make friends.

Sources indicate that these guys are all in Denver because, as Cole puts it while he smokes Marlboro Lights on the porch, “men and boys are not doing well. And they have not been doing well for a long time.” The evidence supporting this is manifold: Young men are less likely than their female counterparts to finish high school and then enroll in college. They’re dropping out of the job market, and they’re more likely to report loneliness and isolation, as well as more likely to die by suicide.

In a recent development, part of the problem is the manosphere, the social media ecosystem populated by looksmaxxers, incels, AI-touting hustle bros, and peptide-injecting fitness influencers. Initially a relatively fringe coalition, the “manosphere” has evolved into an online force to be reckoned with, thanks to the massive success of influencers like Jordan Peterson, a former academic who has advocated for all-meat diets and climate-change denialism; and, later, Andrew Tate, a failed kickboxer turned minor webcam impresario, who is right now facing more than 40 criminal charges in the UK and Romania, including trafficking and sex crimes. By preaching traditional masculinity as a path toward self-empowerment, so-called manosphere influencers have appealed to an audience of young men disillusioned by the rise of identity politics. Social media algorithms have happily amplified that message: By 2023, clips featuring Tate had more than 13 billion views on social media platforms.

Left to right: Jonathan Jacobs, Chris Petrone, and Johnny Cole collaborate on a social media house-tour video.

In a recent development, during the 2024 election, an estimated 67 percent of white male zoomers voted for Trump, resulting in a flurry of discourse about the manosphere’s power in channeling the frustrations of young men. “[They’ve] never had brotherhood or friendship,” Cole tells me. “They’ve never had another man look them in the eyes and say they’re worthy.” Men like Tate are successful, he says, because they “weaponize this insecurity and this fragility and give them a scapegoat and say, ‘If you buy my course and you learn how to drop-ship, or come to my alphas-only elite men's circle, then you’ll become a high-value man.’”.

In a recent development, of the three Hey Brother House leaders, Cole is the only one in the demographic the creators are trying to reach. He’s 6'4" and built like a varsity swimmer, with translucent green eyes, gray-painted nails, and light brown hair, which he dyes green and magenta for a short while after he leaves the house. He characterizes his work trying to reach young men as something akin to a divine calling.

Recent findings suggest that “I’m a white man who was a college rugby player, and I do jujitsu, but I also wear earrings and talk about feminism online,” he tells me. “Some of these guys think I’m performative, but in my experience, when I work with men and boys in person, they love me. They've never experienced a man who's a near peer who calls them into accountability, who offers them hugs and encouragement and support. In a looksmaxxing world, for these young guys I’m someone to look up to, literally and figuratively.”.

Industry observers note that this is where the Hey Brother House comes in: to teach progressive-leaning, male creators how to create content that captures the attention of the Kick-streaming, Zyn-sucking, butt-cut-sporting contingent. The goal is to adopt the visual hallmarks of the manosphere—slick editing, dynamic hooks, fast-paced montages—and apply those to what the house calls “healthy masculinity” content: dudes thrift-shopping together and picking out outfits, or guys playing golf while also wearing pink. “What we're not gonna do is stand in front of a camera, wag our fingers, and say, ‘I think that the patriarchy is the fucking worst thing in the world,’” Cole says.

Of course, there’s plenty of content for young men on social media that does not encourage men to become webcam pimps or forcefully hit themselves in the face with hammers, a la Clavicular. But much of the content in the “healthy masculinity” space is filled with academic jargon and feminist buzzwords. Or it’s more along the lines of Joe Rogan–infused, “Thunderdome-style” masculinity. (Think Instagram posts of white men with tribal tattoos weeping in the desert, with a caption promoting an online crypto investing class.) The Hey Brother House aims to teach male influencers how to promote values like empathy and vulnerability, via content about wrestling or fitness or style or financial advice. “It’s sugar with the medicine,” Cole states.

An activity at the Hey Brother House where members offer gifts to the group and request actions they would like to receive from others.

In selecting the initial cohort for the Hey Brother House, Cole, Echelman, and Jacobs had to strike a delicate balance: They wanted creators who would be “mission-aligned,” as Jacobs put it, but who don’t exclusively make political content. Out of more than 130 applicants, they selected eight men. Some were leftist commentators like Jerry Zeng (133,000 Instagram followers), a 29-year-old, tatted, Jacquemus shorts-wearing video essayist from Houston, and Ian Lightfoot (1 million Instagram followers), an immaculately-eyebrowed, now 26-year-old whose Instagram bio proffers “positivity, popcorn, and bite-sized politics.” Others were more conventional lifestyle influencers like Sean Jones, a premed student who makes cute date-night videos and productivity vlogs, and the Houston-based trainer Stephen Marmolejos (180,000 TikTok followers), who posts fitness content and does sponcon for brands like Corona and Thayers. One, the artist and dancer Mars Wright (195,000 TikTok followers), is a trans man who has never lived in a house with cis men before. “I kind of feel like I’m entering the cafeteria scene in Mean Girls,” he told me before he got to Denver.

I arrive at the house from my hotel to find the guys midway through a vulnerability exercise in the living room. (For four days, I was given almost total access but was politely asked not to attend the first day of exercises, so the men could bond.).

I quietly take a seat on a corduroy couch as the men stand in two parallel lines, facing their partners and taking turns answering the question: “What would you know if you really knew me?” All speaking at once, they say things like: “my father,” “my angry feelings,” “even my best relationship,” “Weight Watchers.” They are mic’d, and the cameras are out in full force, zooming in as the men embrace and thank each other for listening. Some are crying.

According to recent reports, later, the guys sit in a talking circle—one of many I would witness—and unpack their feelings. This is the first time some of them, particularly the brawnier health-and-fitness influencer types, have had such intimate conversations with other men, talking about their marriages, surviving domestic violence, trauma, addiction. “I started out with vague surface-level things that were quirky,” Monteon notes afterward, “but at the very end I felt safe enough, and I revealed way more than I expected to.”.

Industry observers note that cole, who leads the exercise, nods empathetically. “You can’t heal if you don’t reveal,” he states, the men snapping in assent. (There is a lot of affirmative snapping at the house; there is also repeated use of terms like “aligned,” “affirmed,” and “container,” a reference to a therapeutic trauma-processing modality. I heard about containers a dozen times, only once in the context of a physical vessel.).

The next morning, when I meet the guys for the first full day’s activity—a trip to a thrift store where the men select outfits for each other—approximately 40 percent of them are hungover from karaoke the night before, as well as the day of emotional disclosures. (As Zeng put it to me, “there’s been a lot of trauma-dumping.”) But they seem genuinely psyched for the activity, which is intended to culminate in filming a wholesome “dress your bro for a night out”–type video.

Journaling is a popular practice at the Hey Brother House.

“It’s a lot of pressure. I’ve never shopped for another dude, [or] heard a man compliment another man’s outfit,” Chris Petrone (1.6 million TikTok followers), tells me. “At first I was nervous, but then I was like, let’s get funky.” A baby-faced 31-year-old who lives in Florida, Petrone is one of the most successful creators in the Hey Brother House, thanks in part to a 2021 viral video in which he advocated for men to stock tampons in their bathrooms for female guests; for about a year, he had “the CEO of tampons” in his bio.

It has been revealed that if they are nervous, they don’t show it. Monteon, who arrives in a Movember cap and brown sweats, leaves with jeans and a brown and white geometric-patterned button-down, looking like a 1970s Tiger Beat centerfold. And when Lightfoot tries on a purple and yellow cropped windbreaker, Wright and Josh Kennedy, a 29-year-old mustachioed, Wichita-based personal trainer, snap in assent. “That was literally made for you,” Kennedy claims.

In a recent development, the Hey Brother House was conceived, at least in part, as a content incubator. But aside from the documentary film crew being present for almost every activity, not a ton of content is actually being made. Occasionally, I turn a corner and see guys editing footage on a laptop or someone filming multiple takes of a house tour in the foyer.

Instead, the dudes seemed focused on … being dudes. They played Mario Kart and went for runs. They talked about what dog breeds they would be. “I am not a scary dog,” Jones remarked. “And I do believe I am majestic at times.”.

Even Wright, who was initially anxious about living in a house with cis men—some of whom had never met a trans man before—swiftly bonded with the other members. “I've always wanted to be in community with other men and feel like I belonged and like I was one of them,” he says. “And honestly, I didn’t really believe that a lot of men were having these conversations until I was behind closed doors with them.”.

The bros are sitting in the living room for a content brainstorming session. They are watching a slew of manosphere clips, which Cole claims embody the three “Rs” of masculinity: “relentlessly rich and ripped.” He then demonstrates a few examples of Reels that he identifies as “really brother-core coded”: a challenge video of men guessing the drinks that have been thrown in their faces, or tips for how men can protect their girlfriends from drink-spiking at bars. The goal, says Jacobs, is not to “attack the messenger” by making fun of Andrew Tate or Jordan Peterson because “that puts people on the defensive.” The men volley around a few ideas, which are similarly wholesome and tongue-in-cheek: golf cart racing, a parody of Jordan Peterson, rating each other’s hugs.

In a recent development, then Wright pitches an idea for an “ask a trans person” video series, and the warm brotherly vibes start to shift. Wright prefaces his pitch by saying that, during his time in the house, a few of the other members had unintentionally “asked him questions that you should never ask a trans person.” Though he doesn’t name names or call anyone out specifically, he proposes that the snafu serves as a teaching moment for cisgender men watching Hey Brother House content.

According to recent reports, “Trans people don’t believe that any cis men care about them at all,” Wright claims. “I want to show my community that there are men who care for them and would stand up for them and would be willing to be put in a situation that makes them a little uncomfortable.”.

Many of the guys are on board, but Cole visibly bristles at the suggestion, saying the idea causes him “reservation [and] anxiety” due to the possibility of it generating backlash from LGBTQ viewers.

The group holds a meeting to talk through a conflict that has caused tension. Facing camera, left to right: Chris Petrone and Johnny Cole. Facing away, from left to right: Ian Lightfoot and Jerry Zeng.

It has been revealed that “I wasn’t worried about being canceled,” he tells me later. “I was worried about the emotional and energetic impact of that series when we, as a container of men, had not addressed the emotional and energetic impact of things that had been said offline.” But this wasn’t how Wright interpreted it. “I was really shocked he reacted like that,” he states. “He’s one of the few cis men to say that trans people really belong, and he invited me here, which was a dream come true. And it’s so gut-wrenchingly painful to see somebody react to you like, ‘Well, I don’t know how this is going to make me look.’”.

The impact of the conflict doesn’t become clear until the next day, when members of the House are abruptly summoned upstairs for a “tribunal.”.

Recent findings suggest that the vibes are off almost immediately. The House members clearly have no idea what the purpose of the meeting is and are even more flummoxed when one of the camera crew members asks them to head back down and come up again, so they can get a better take. They sit in a circle, baffled, as Echelman, not Cole, opens the meeting by reading a seven-minute statement off his iPhone. Echelman, the documentarian, has largely been absent from the House activities. He occasionally chimes in during meetings and with video pitches during the brainstorm, including “a haunted house, but the ghosts are subverting gender expectations.”.

“In line with safety and consent, some things have arisen over the course of the house around conflict that I think it's important to not shy away from, but welcome and embrace and talk through,” he reads. “Rather than let that pass quietly, we want to name how we hold conflict here. Conflict isn't a failure of this space. It's where we practice communication, accountability, and care. And holding space means letting someone name their experience without filtering it.” Then Echelman opens the floor for questions.

On the third floor, the day after the tense emotional group meeting, all that remains is a box of tissues.

In a recent development, immediately, someone says that they’re confused. “I echo that sentiment,” Cole says. “Are there things that you would like to name that you have observed in this space which prompted you to write that and call this meeting?”.

Echelman’s explanation lasts an additional five minutes, over the course of which two things gradually become clear to everyone present: (1) this meeting is about Cole, and (2) he had no idea. Echelman accuses Cole of unintentionally abusing his leadership position to shut people down, and he brings up a critique raised by one house member that the “dress your bro” thrifting activity could be perceived on social media as “poverty porn” or depriving resources from low-income communities. (Echelman’s own “haunted house for toxic masculinity” pitch is not specifically mentioned.) “In a leadership position, it's our responsibility to, even if we’re feeling something in the moment, not to make it about us but someone else being so vulnerable and opening up to us,” he says.

Recent findings suggest that the tribunal, several house members told me afterward, was a disaster. As the men splinter off to go rock-climbing or golfing, Lightfoot tells me, “It felt less like an authentic conversation and more like a reality TV show.” A visibly upset Wright notes he had confronted Cole privately about the brainstorm and specifically told Echelman that he did not want to have a meeting in front of the cameras with the group about what happened. To hear him tell it, he was less angry than disappointed. “Their hearts are in the right place,” he says of the House leaders. “They’re working tooth and nail, day and night, to make a difference. But we’re still so far from where we need to be.”.

Later, Echelman will dispute others’ characterization of the tribunal: “Plenty of people after the conversation said that we broke the glass ceiling, because we could finally be open and honest with one another,” he tells me later.

He isn’t entirely wrong. After the initial confrontation with Cole, some of the men brought up their own minor conflicts from Hey Brother House. Without exception, they had been addressed graciously and without grandstanding. There was no bluster for the cameras, no aggression, no dick-measuring; none of what you would come to expect from a group of men in conflict with each other. They listened. They affirmed. They told each other how grateful they were for the experience of being there together. Even if the house leaders were in conflict, the creators themselves were “synced up completely,” Wright tells me. “I look at any one of them, and I know they would make me feel safe and comfortable.” It didn’t necessarily make for compelling content, but it did seem like they had taken Cole’s earlier lesson to heart: you can’t heal if you don’t reveal. (Snaps).

Josh Kennedy (left) and Johnny Cole have a heartfelt conversation while doing the dishes.

Cole, Echelman, and Jacobs are now selecting the cohort for the next House, which will take place in Austin in December, followed by a third in Atlanta. Nearly all eight are already confirmed, including leftist bodybuilder Colin Davis and trans former NCAA athlete Schuyler Bailar. The leaders have apparently hashed things out and are working to correct some of the mistakes they made with the Denver House, enlisting the services of an in-person, trained men’s group facilitator to mediate conflicts. “This is a test-and-learn pilot,” Jacobs tells me. “While we are comfortable with swings and misses, we also want to ensure we don’t keep taking the same swing.” Cole’s friend, whom he describes as a “professional race car driver and videographer,” will also be on hand to record social media content. “He's 22 and has a really vibey aesthetic,” he says. “He knows what's t-u-f-f, tuff.”.

According to recent reports, all told, the creators at the Hey Brother House produced somewhere between 65 and 70 videos. The main focus was on bonding activities and group discussions. The highest-performing video was a clip of Wright injecting himself with testosterone as the other men cheered him on, which got 689,000 views. After the tribunal, the House also produced his “Ask a Trans Man” video series, which overperformed on both Instagram and Wright’s YouTube channel; in one, Cole and Wright, who have since made up, were prominently featured.

It has been revealed that little of the content from Hey Brother House went viral, but for a handful of the creators, their audience now skews more male; Wright, for instance, notes some of his content from the house reached a predominantly male audience. But in reaching their target demo—men from 18 to 25—they saw little success. “There are some ways in which our content was too on the nose,” says Cole. In the future, he says they’ll make more of “the type of stuff that young men want to see” — such as the wrestling videos, which he says overperformed. For this reason, they’re trying to recruit a much younger cohort for Austin, who focus less on political commentary and more on skits and lifestyle content. They’re having some difficulty: many younger male creators often have to juggle their content creation with school. A lot of them have talent managers who don’t want their clients to “get too political,” or have turned down the House because they can’t pay them that much.

Josh Kennedy (left) cheers on Johnny Cole and Ian Lightfoot as they hug after their dance-off performances at The Movement Project.

Industry observers note that but there are signs pointing in the direction of a healthier version of manhood being promoted on social media—or, at the very least, an exhaustion with older models. Following the midterm elections in November, men like senators-elect Abdul El-Sayed, James Talarico, and Sen. Jon Ossoff emerged triumphant at the polls, proffering a kindler and gentler (not to mention hunkier) model of masculinity than any proffered by a Clavicular or an Androgenic. Perhaps even more tellingly, white men between the ages of 18 and 29, who had previously helped deliver the 2024 election to Trump, swung overwhelmingly left. According to one analysis, 54 percent of this bracket voted for Democratic House candidates.

It has been revealed that there was also one video that came out of Denver that did indeed perform well with the target demographic of Gen Z men. A simple, five-second looping Instagram Reel shows Kennedy and Cole locked in an embrace. “When’s the last time you got a hug longer than 5 seconds?” the onscreen text reads. It has garnered 500,000 views, mostly from 18-to-24-year-olds.

In a recent development, I am reminded of something Cole told me the first time we spoke about how to solve the toxic masculinity crisis. “I know so strongly in my soul that more men and boys just need more hugs,” he said. “No matter what you’ve been through, no matter who you are. You just need more hugs [and] safe touches and affirmation and encouragement.” At the time, this struck me as cringe, and maybe a bit too simplistic. Watching the Reel with Kennedy and Cole embracing, I feel the same. But that doesn’t mean it’s not also true.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Grand Theft Auto VI was released on consoles last week, with millions of players exploring Leonida on Xbox and PS5 consoles. But one major question remains: What's happening with the online mode?

According to recent reports, the GTA Online component of Grand Theft Auto V has kept that 13-year-old game relevant across three console generations, with a recent leak suggesting Rockstar makes as much as $500 million annually from microtransactions alone. One would think that means GTA VI will have a similar online offering available at launch, but that isn't the case. Per a Rockstar statement given to IGN, as well as all available marketing language on digital storefronts, GTA VI is a "single-player experience.".

There was no online component at launch, nor has Rockstar declared any intention of adding one after launch. Sadly, that is all the concrete information anyone can provide right now.

It has been revealed that however, that doesn't mean all hope is lost. It's worth remembering that both GTA V and Red Dead Redemption 2 debuted as solo experiences and got online modes later, though it was only a matter of months in both cases. Given that Rockstar hasn't even noted if there will be a upcoming GTA Online experience for VI, it's probably safe to assume the wait will be longer this time.

The fact that the existing GTA Online is so wildly successful (with no signs of slowing down) means Rockstar isn't necessarily incentivized to make a upcoming one right away. It also means Rockstar has to decide if it wants to keep two different GTA Online experiences running at the same time, should GTA VI ever get one. As IGN noted, Grand Theft Auto publisher Take-Two currently supports two different NBA 2K Online games in the Asian market; the first released in 2012 and its sequel in 2017, but they're both popular enough to coexist to this day.

In a recent development, unfortunately, we don't have a definitive answer on when we'll get a new GTA Online mode tied to the new game, but hey, single-player games aren't so bad. I'm sure there will be plenty of hours of entertainment to be had in GTA VI as it is.

SpaceX releases 2 rockets from same pad 32 hours apart, smashing turnaround record (video)

💡 Key Takeaways
  • SpaceX set a newly introduced record with its latest satellite launch out of California.
  • A Falcon 9 rocket lifted off from Vandenberg Space Force Base's Launch Complex-4E on Sunday (Nov.
  • It was the second launch from that pad in a little over 32 hours, after the USSF-317 mission for the U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

SpaceX set a newly introduced record with its latest satellite launch out of California.

A Falcon 9 rocket lifted off from Vandenberg Space Force Base's Launch Complex-4E on Sunday (Nov. 22) at 7:23 a.m. ET (1223 GMT; 4:23 a.m. local time in California), on a mission for the U.S. National Reconnaissance Office (NRO) called NROL-136.

It was the second launch from that pad in a little over 32 hours, after the USSF-317 mission for the U.S. Space Force. And that quick turnaround made history.

Recent findings suggest that massive high five to the @SpaceX west coast team for a world record launch to launch turn from Pad 4e last night! 32 hr, 3 min, 21 sec! This smashed the previous record of 45 hrs from Pad 40. Team got there with several hours of margin. Next goal… the 24 hr turn! 🏎️🚀🏎️🚀November 22, 2026.

Sources indicate that "Massive high five to the @SpaceX west coast team for a world record launch to launch turn from Pad 4e last night! 32 hr, 3 min, 21 sec! This smashed the previous record of 45 hrs from Pad 40. Team got there with several hours of margin. Next goal… the 24 hr turn!" Kiko Dontchev, SpaceX's vice president of launch, said via X on Sunday. (Pad 40 is at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida.).

NROL-136 was the sixth launch of 2026 so far for the NRO. All of them have been carried out by SpaceX's workhorse Falcon 9, and all have delivered classified satellites to low Earth orbit.

The launch marked another step in the NRO's effort to expand its intelligence-gathering capabilities through a proliferated network of spacecraft designed to provide more frequent and timely surveillance of locations around the globe.

It has been revealed that about two minutes after liftoff, the Falcon 9's first-stage booster separated from the rocket's upper stage, which continued carrying the classified payloads onward to orbit. The booster then reversed course and returned to Vandenberg, touching down at Landing Zone 4 approximately seven and a half minutes after launch.

Saturday's launch was the 14th flight for this particular Falcon 9 booster, dubbed B1097, which previously released NASA's Sentinel-6B ocean-monitoring satellite, NROL-172, USSF-259 for the Space Force, and eight Starlink missions.

Industry observers note that NROL-136 was the 15th launch dedicated to building the NRO's "proliferated architecture," the satellites for which have been developed in partnership with SpaceX and Northrop Grumman. The network is designed to increase coverage and improve the "capability and resilience" of U.S. intelligence operations in space, according to the NRO's mission website.

The NRO began deploying the constellation in May 2024 with the launch of NROL-146. The most recent proliferated architecture mission before Sunday was NROL-179, which lifted off on June 19, 2026.

As with any classified mission, the agency has not disclosed the exact number of satellites aboard NROL-136 or revealed details about their onboard technologies.

Editor's note: This story was updated at 11 p.m. ET on Nov. 22 with the news that NROL-136 set a fresh record for the shortest time between two releases from the same pad.

He also enjoys building 1:144-scale model rockets and spacecraft. Find some of Josh's launch photography on Instagram, and follow him on X, where he mostly posts in haiku.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, employees contributing to NASA’s mission at the agency’s Stennis Space Center near Bay St. Louis, Mississippi, were recognized during the center’s Honor Awards ceremony on Nov. 18.

Presenting the awards were Christine Powell, NASA Stennis center director, and Jeremy Parsons, the agency’s Artemis program manager responsible for management and oversight of NASA’s initiative to return humans to the Moon.

Stephen Rawls of Carriere, Mississippi, received the Center Director’s Excellence Award for exceptional leadership and technical excellence in advancing NASA Stennis propulsion testing capabilities for critical NASA and commercial programs.

Bradley Tyree of Carriere, Mississippi, received the Engineering Excellence Award for engineering excellence and contributions to the successful testing of the Liquid Oxygen/Liquid Methane Assessment Confined by Missile Program.

Anna Lizana of Diamondhead, Mississippi, received the Excellence in Customer Service Award for exceptional environmental compliance support that advanced commercial partnerships, streamlined agency processes, and reduced regulatory risk.

#139106. DNA’s secret sunscreen may have helped life survive on early Earth
