Last year, GOP Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene of Georgia spoke at a white nationalist event organized by Holocaust denier Nick Fuentes that caused Republican leaders to denounce her.

Last week, Greene’s Twitter account was temporarily suspended by the Elon Musk-headed platform over a tweet with a graphic referring to a “Trans Day of Vengeance,” as she denounced a planned transgender rights rally.

And come Tuesday, Greene has declared prepares to protest in Upcoming York City when former President Donald Trump is expected to be arraigned on an indictment of more than 30 counts, calling the proceedings against him an “unconstitutional WITCH HUNT!”.

In a recent development, but on Sunday, Greene was featured on CBS’ “60 Minutes” in an interview the long-running show promoted on Twitter with the tease: “Republican Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene, nicknamed MTG, isn’t afraid to share her opinions, no matter how intense and in-your-face they are. She sits down with Lesley Stahl this Sunday on 60 Minutes.” The images attached to this tweet by “60 Minutes” include Greene and Stahl walking through the US Capitol, taking a stroll outside and Greene showing Stahl something on her phone.

It's time for Marjorie Taylor Greene to go.

In the segment that aired Sunday night, Stahl noted the congresswoman had moved from the fringe to the GOP’s front row in two years despite a “sharp tongue” and “some pretty radical views” as well as “over the top” comments such as “the Democrats are a party of pedophiles.” Stahl also referred to video of Greene chasing a Parkland, Florida, school shooting survivor, still maintaining that the 2020 election was stolen and failing to criticize Trump over spending. (The interview was conducted before news of his indictment.).

But Stahl didn’t mention Greene spoke at a white nationalist event a year ago while a member of Congress or her extreme anti-Muslim views and her defense of January 6 rioters.

Recent findings suggest that criticism of CBS for amplifying Greene has been swift and well-deserved even before the program aired. Former GOP Rep. Adam Kinzinger of Illinois tweeted beforehand: “Wow. Insane that 60 min would do this.” (Kinzinger is a CNN senior political commentator.).

Journalist Molly Jong-Fast also slammed “60 Minutes” with the tweet: “Attention is currency and 60 minutes is spending its currency on the Jewish space lasers woman.” (Jong-Fast was apparently referring to Greene’s past claim that a massive California wildfire was started by “a laser” beamed from space controlled by a prominent Jewish banking family.).

David Hogg, who survived the 2018 horrific school shooting at Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School in Parkland and has since become an activist against gun violence, responded, “I look forward to your questions about why she thinks school shootings are fake and why she’s supported QAnon.”.

Trump's risky call for protests.

Greene amplified the conspiracy theory — two years before being elected to Congress — that the Parkland shooting that took 17 lives was staged. And in 2019, Greene appeared on video confronting Hogg outside the Capitol when he was championing laws to save lives from gun violence, screaming that the then-teenager was a “coward.” She also called Hogg “#littleHitler” on social media.

Greene’s own tweet promoting Sunday’s segment was not filled with her typical smears of “fake news” when she doesn’t like the coverage. Rather, Greene urged people to tune in as she praised “60 Minutes” host Stahl (and misspelled her first name): “It was an honor to spend a few days with the legendary icon Leslie Stahl and talented crew @60Minutes.” Greene added, “Leslie is a trailblazer for women in journalism. And while we may disagree on some issues, I respect her greatly.”.

In a recent development, now, it is true that “60 Minutes” over its 50-plus-year history has featured what the show has dubbed “controversial” guests. These include a 2000 interview with Oklahoma City bomber Timothy McVeigh, whose 1995 terrorist attack left 168 dead, including 19 children. And the show did a 1979 interview with Iran’s Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini.

Industry observers note that perhaps “60 Minutes” views Greene — who has repeatedly downplayed and even defended the January 6, 2021, attack plus called for the GOP to become the party of “Christian nationalism” — in the vein of its long list of controversial guests. (CBS had not responded to a request from CNN for comment at time of publishing.).

Join us on Twitter and Facebook.

However, the choice of Greene as a guest instantly recalls the comments of then-CBS CEO Les Moonves during Trump’s 2016 presidential campaign when he admitted that Trump’s candidacy “may not be good for America, but it’s damn good for CBS.” Moonves added, “The money’s rolling in and this is fun. … (T)his is going to be a very good year for us,” concluding, “Sorry. It’s a terrible thing to say. But bring it on, Donald. Keep going.”.

Moonves may be gone from CBS, but it appears his mindset continues at “60 Minutes.” And that may be good for “60 Minutes,” but it’s definitely not good for America.

Industry observers note that I didn’t expect much as I unboxed the Brainstorm Night Sky; after all, I’m significantly older than this educational star projector’s target audience. Perhaps I’d come away with a sense of wonder and delight, coupled with mild irritation at having to hunt down three AA batteries to power it.

Instead, I was filled with envy as the Brainstorm Night Sky reminded me just what I was missing, thanks to the rigors of light pollution. A few minutes after powering it down, I was already making plans for my first dark sky trip, yearning for a view that rivaled the Brainstorm’s cosmic images.

Industry observers note that draw the curtains, press the Night Sky’s single button (tilting the projector and twisting the focus as appropriate) and it projects a circular image onto a ceiling or wall. Press the button again and the projection slowly begins to rotate, slowly but stutter-free. It really is that simple to operate and, aimed at budding astronomers aged eight or above, it's reasonably lightweight without feeling flimsy.

Weight: 14.8 oz (420 g)Bulb type: Non-specifiedLaser: NoControl: On-unitRotation: Yes, one speedProjection area: Up to 8.2 ft (2.5 m)Sleep timer: Yes (30 mins)Power: 3x AA batteries Speaker: No.

I was initially a little surprised by the size of the projection: at up to 8.2 feet (2.5 m) wide it’s not going to fill an entire ceiling. It also switches off after 30 minutes, a limit that can’t be disabled, so if you’re looking to put on your own space-themed party this is not the projector for you. But it’s on point for home education and, priced from $49.99, the Brainstorm Night Sky projector won’t break the bank.

Recent findings suggest that there’s minimal distortion around the edge of the images; the planets are spherical from the word go, unlike some projectors where I’ve had to tweak them to stop Mars turning into an egg. And I never once had to crane my neck because half the solar system had been projected onto a bookcase.

In a recent development, the Brainstorm Night Sky model I tested comes with four slides, each with a case to protect them from smudges and sticky fingers. You place one into the provided slide housing then insert that into the projector. There’s the moon, the solar system, and two showing the Northern Hemisphere’s night sky, as seen from Hawaii (a key location for astronomy).

In a recent development, I can appreciate the educational value of the first couple, even if I am still seething at Pluto being demoted back in 2006. But it was the latter pair of slides that really opened my eyes to what I could be seeing over my head.

I can spot maybe 10-20 stars from my backyard, cloud cover permitting; thanks to light pollution, that’s it. Even though the best stargazing apps can show me what I should see, when I step outside, all I typically see with the naked eye is the odd pinprick in the void.

But as soon as I inserted that third slide, a striking stellar display appeared above my head, with more stars than I could hope to count. Even knowing that Hawaii’s night sky stretches far further than eight feet across, the difference between this view and the one from my house was like night and day. Brainstorm claims this slide features over 20,000 stars, though that’s likely referring to the source photo rather than the projected image.

In a recent development, the fourth slide — the same crisp starscape but with every visible constellation labelled — was almost as attention-grabbing. Educational value aside, it drove home that I couldn’t see the majority of these star patterns to name them, my local night sky is that polluted.

According to recent reports, knowing what I was missing out on made me determined to take my stargazing further afield. Some of the best smart telescopes can lessen the impact of light pollution, but stepping away from skyglow is the most effective option. Hawaii’s a little far to travel, but I’ve already started looking into local dark sky sites. I just need to grab a pair of the best binoculars for stargazing, hop on my bike and I’m ready to go.

Industry observers note that the Brainstorm Night Sky’s projections are crisp enough that you can easily make out every constellation name, but they could be a hair brighter. The Ainael Meter Galaxy Projector, for example, delivers more illumination.

In a recent development, if you want to use the Brainstorm Night Sky to relax, the rotate function gives its projections an oddly hypnotic effect, and the device is whisper-quiet to boot. And while Brainstorm doesn’t specify battery life, one set of rechargeables lasted me for several days.

According to recent reports, unfortunately, the Brainstorm Night Sky's slide collection is a little limited. There are two models, a blue version with four slides (the one I tested) and a gray version with six slides (featuring additional space shuttle and black hole images). The included instructions state you can purchase an additional slide disc showing the Southern Hemisphere’s stars, but that’s a maximum of seven images. Nor is this projector compatible with the slides from the Brainstorm Deep Sky Projector.

Sources indicate that it’s a little disappointing given that Brainstorm has clearly put thought into the projector’s educational value. Those instructions double as a poster of the solar system, and children can use a “secret code” (printed on the instructions) to explore more astronomy facts on the tech giant’s website.

Offering extra slide packs, of the kind you can buy for the Pococo Galaxy Projector, would give it more long-term appeal. As is, I can see its novelty and educational value diminishing over time, at which point you can upgrade to one of the best star projectors.

According to recent reports, if you’re not bothered by the lack of expandability, the Brainstorm Night Sky’s price, image quality and ease of use still make it a useful tool for kindling a child’s interest in astronomy, or as a budget-friendly gift for junior stargazers. It’s certainly spurred me into action — how much is a plane ticket to Hawaii, anyway?

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In an open letter to the CEOs of Amazon and eBay, a coalition of 155 child advocacy groups called on the online marketplaces to stop selling toys powered by artificial intelligence.

The letter argues that AI toys are "cheap, easy to buy, and largely untested." It lists numerous risks associated with the products, including sexually explicit content, unproven educational claims, privacy violations, and instructions for how to access and use harmful household items.

The letter's publication follows the release of annual toy research conducted by U.S. PIRG. While some AI products made crucial safety gains compared to last year, others still have inappropriate conversations and pose considerable privacy risks.

The Alilo Smart AI Bunny, for example, told a tester where to search in their house for bleach, defined the word "fetish," discussed specific sexual scenarios, explained why lubricant can be helpful, and suggested using "padded cuffs, soft floggers, or feather ticklers.".

Amazon subsequently removed the bunny and another toy capable of sexual exchanges from its platform. The letter identified over 50 AI toys available for sale on Amazon's U.S. marketplace.

"These products should be shown to be safe before they reach children, not withdrawn one at a time after harm is found," the letter remarked.

The effort was led by the child advocacy groups Fairplay, Alliance 4 Children CIC, and Set@16. On Friday, Amazon told U.S. PIRG that it had removed toys as it investigated the alleged concerns.

"Amazon is committed to the safety of children and families," the company mentioned in a statement to PIRG. "We're working with our partners across the industry and government to ensure proper guardrails for these products are in place as this technology develops.".

eBay responded to the open letter in response to Mashable's request for comment.

"We are committed to protecting the buyers and sellers on our marketplace and we continually evaluate our policies and engage with regulators to ensure our marketplace remains safe, trusted, and responsive to evolving safety standards," an eBay spokesperson remarked in an email.

Amazon told Mashable that it requires all products sold by third-parties to comply with applicable laws and regulations.

"Amazon is committed to the safety of children and families," the company stated in an email. "We support efforts across the industry and government to put appropriate guardrails in place as this technology develops.".

The letter notes that California banned toys with companion chatbots for children younger than 16, beginning Jan. 2027. A bill introduced in Congress would also ban AI chatbots in toys.

"You do not need to wait," the letter noted, addressing Amazon and eBay. "Marketplaces are responsible for the safety of what they sell, and you already remove unsafe products.".

Explanation: What creates the colors in Jupiter's clouds? No one is sure. The thick atmosphere of Jupiter is mostly hydrogen and helium, elements which are colorless at the low temperatures of the Jovian cloud tops. Which trace molecules provide the colors remains a topic of research, although small amounts of ammonium hydrosulfide are one leading candidate. What is clear from the featured color-enhanced image -- and many similar images -- is that lighter clouds are typically higher up than darker ones. Pictured, light clouds swirl around reddish regions toward the lower right, while they appear to cover over some darker domains on the upper right. The featured image was taken by the robotic Juno spacecraft in 2018 during its 14th low pass over Jupiter. Juno continues in its looping elliptical orbit, swooping near the huge planet every 33 days and exploring a slightly different sector each time around.Tomorrow's picture: emerging darkness.

#139078. What did the Soviet Union's final deep space probe actually see on Mars?

What did the Soviet Union's final deep space probe actually see on Mars?

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1557 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Space

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • On July 12, 1988, Phobos 2 — one of the Soviet Union's final major planetary exploration probes — was launched from Baikonur Cosmodrome aboard a Proton rocket.
  • According to recent reports, however, early in the following year, the spacecraft's mission abruptly ended after the Phobos 2 ground team mysteriously lost contact with the spacecraft.
  • So what caused the odd-looking appearance of the shadow in the final images captured by Phobos 2, and what was the real reason behind the spacecraft's sudden failure?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On July 12, 1988, Phobos 2 — one of the Soviet Union's final major planetary exploration probes — was launched from Baikonur Cosmodrome aboard a Proton rocket. The spacecraft's mission included the study of Mars and the Martian moon Phobos, with a planned close approach and deployment of landing probes, and over the next several months, the spacecraft successfully captured more than three dozen images of Phobos during its time in service.

According to recent reports, however, early in the following year, the spacecraft's mission abruptly ended after the Phobos 2 ground team mysteriously lost contact with the spacecraft. Adding to the mystery were objects in some of the final photographs dispatched by the doomed spacecraft, which seemed to show an elongated shadow beneath the probe — a strange twist in one of the Soviet Union's final space missions, and one that soon gave rise to conspiracy theories about what the fate of Phobos 2 might have been.

So what caused the odd-looking appearance of the shadow in the final images captured by Phobos 2, and what was the real reason behind the spacecraft's sudden failure?

Originally, the Soviet Union had planned for Phobos 2 to reach the Red Planet by late January 1989, after which the spacecraft would begin collecting data about the Martian environment leading up to its initial contact with Mars' largest moon in early June.

Sources indicate that to say that a lot hinged on the success of the mission would be an understatement, given the unfortunate fate of the probe's predecessor, Phobos 1, which went offline on Sept. 2, 1988, after a faulty command sequence was initiated while the spacecraft was on its way to Mars. The stakes were almost immediately raised as Phobos 2 arrived in orbit around Mars on Jan. 30, 1989, when one of the probe's three onboard flight system processors was found to have gone offline, with another already experiencing technical concerns.

In a recent development, over the course of the next several weeks, Phobos 2 was able to overcome some of these setbacks and successfully began sending useful scientific data about the Martian environment back to Earth. By March, all the probe's science instruments appeared to be functioning normally, and despite the earlier loss of one of its processors, the remaining two had continued to facilitate control of the spacecraft by its Soviet ground control team.

That all changed on March 27, 1989, as Phobos 2 prepared to capture navigational images of its namesake as the Martian moon passed, which would be useful in advance of another forthcoming flyby in early April.

Achieving this meant that the probe had to be angled in such a way that it faced Phobos, whereby its communications antennas would be temporarily directed away from Earth. During the imaging portion of the maneuver, all appeared to go smoothly, but soon afterward, ground controllers realized they were unable to reestablish contact with the probe.

In a recent development, A few fleeting radio contacts were made over the ensuing hours, which engineers believed might indicate that during the period of signal loss required for imagery of Phobos to be obtained, the spacecraft may have begun to spin uncontrollably. If this were the case, and the spacecraft could not reorient its solar panels toward the sun, it would eventually lose all power.

Industry observers note that no further contact with Phobos 2 could be established beyond this point, although images from the probe's final close encounter with the Martian moon were successfully delivered back to Soviet ground controllers. While investigators identified a failure involving the spacecraft's onboard computer system as the most probable explanation, to this day, the exact cause of the events leading to the loss remains unknown.

In a recent development, although questions remain about the fate of Phobos 2, several theories have been put forward over the years. According to authors Paolo Ulivi and David M. Harland, one of the simplest explanations was that the spacecraft was damaged after an impact with other material orbiting the Martian moon, although later modeling by Soviet engineers and American teams at NASA's Jet Propulsion Lab seemed to rule this out.

A more likely scenario involved failure of the probe's second attitude control computer, which had already begun experiencing technical issues as Phobos 2 arrived in Martian orbit. With two of its three processors now offline, the third and sole remaining computer was unable to maintain control of the spacecraft on its own. An additional factor might have been power loss from battery drainage while the probe's solar arrays were directed away from the sun, and with no failsafe to power down any non-critical systems under such conditions, the spacecraft would likely have undergone significant power loss.

However, the probe's failure was only one part of the mystery: equally perplexing had been the unusual images Phobos 2 captured in its final moments, which later sparked speculation — and conspiracy theories — about what might have been behind the spacecraft's sudden demise.

In some of the final images captured by Phobos 2, an unusual, elongated shadow had been visible in the frame, which with time would begin to prompt the most unusual of all the theories about the probe's demise: that it had been disabled by an alien spacecraft.

Sources indicate that among the proponents of this theory had been Marina Popovich, a former experimental pilot and the first Soviet woman to break the sound barrier, who set over 100 world aviation records in her career. In 1991, Popovich held a press conference at the Soviet Consulate in San Francisco, where she claimed a cigar-shaped object had been photographed near the Martian moon, which she believed to be an alien mothership.

In a recent development, given her storied background in Soviet aerospace history, Popovich's views likely carried a degree of credibility unlike most others. However, that did not make them accurate.

Recent findings suggest that determining what the images actually show requires an understanding of the probe's orbit, particularly with relation to the Martian moon it was attempting to photograph. At the time, the spacecraft and Phobos were in almost the same orbit, and moving at very similar speeds. As Ulivi and Harland note, due to these conditions, the probe's Termoskan multispectral imager often captured images that "included the shadow of the moon on the planet's surface as a dark oblong cigar-shaped feature.".

In 1991, a NASA-led study of the Termoskan observations concluded that the unusual appearance of the shadow most likely resulted from a combination of factors acting together. The study team attributed these to the scanning instrument itself, as well as the spacecraft's near-co-orbital motion with Phobos, its viewing direction, and finally, a slight rocking motion the researchers concluded the spacecraft had likely exhibited at the time.

However, another factor that contributed to the appearance of the shadow involves the oblique angle at which the moon's shadow strikes the Martian surface. Because of this, similar imagery depicting an elliptical or elongated shadow cast by Phobos has been obtained since the Phobos 2 mission, with examples including images captured by the High-Resolution Stereo Camera (HRSC) on the ESA's Mars Express spacecraft in 2005.

The loss of Phobos 2 became a controversy for reasons other than the imaginative speculations about what its final images might have captured.

Sources indicate that john M. Logsdon, director of the Space Policy Institute at George Washington University's School of International Affairs, remarked to the Los Angeles Times shortly after the failure that the situation was "just horrible," noting that the mishap was expected to potentially fuel what he called "a first-rate bureaucratic struggle" the Soviet Union was undergoing amid political changes occurring there at the time.

"The scientific community is also facing challenges resulting from the restructuring of the Soviet system," the Times also reported, noting the scientists from more than a dozen nations around the world whose funding and scientific instruments, at an estimated cost of several millions of dollars, "must be counted among the losers in the failure of the probe to complete its basic mission.".

Recent findings suggest that although both Phobos spacecraft were lost prior to completion of their primary missions, there were still some meaningful scientific results they produced. These included new data collected about both Mars and Phobo­s which, according to Ulivi and Harland, exceeded the total data collected from all past Soviet missions to the Red Planet.

Ultimately, the circumstances surrounding the demise of Phobos 2 remain one of the more intriguing episodes in the history of Soviet space exploration. The unusual observations made during its final moments, coupled with lingering questions about precisely what went wrong, have helped sustain decades of speculation.

In a recent development, today, the truncated Phobos 2 mission remains a curious ending note for the Soviet-era space program. It is one that still fuels speculation, and reminds us how rapidly the unknown can take our minds to imaginative places — especially when it comes to mysteries involving space, the cosmos, and the potential existence of life beyond Earth.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The European Union and Indonesia signed a free trade deal on Saturday, describing it as a newly introduced chapter in economic relations between the two sides.

"This is one of the most ambitious deals the European Union has concluded in Asia," Ursula von der Leyen, president of the European Commission, stated at the signing ceremony on Saturday.

"Together, we represent a market of 730 million people," she added.

The Indonesia-European Union Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA) and the additional Investment Protection Agreement (IPA) are designed to reduce trade barriers and attract investment in strategic sectors such as electric vehicles, electronics, and pharmaceuticals.

The agreement comes after almost 10 years of negotiations and is part of a wider series of trade deals by the EU.

The bloc hopes to reduce its reliance on individual economic partners as trade with both China and the US has become more difficult in recent years.

Von der Leyen also stressed the importance of international cooperation, saying that "in a time when others are closing their doors, we keep ours open.".

Recent findings suggest that the deal sees tariffs on about 98% of EU exports to Indonesia to be done away with. The EU estimates that European companies could save more than €600 million (around $658 million) per year.

"The benefits for our exporters are concrete and measurable," Indonesian Minister of Economic Affairs Airlangga Hartarto stated, hailing a "new chapter" in economic relations with the EU. He said the deal would benefit his country’s main exports to Europe, including palm oil, footwear and textiles.

Palm oil and deforestation had been major stumbling blocks during the negotiations, and the agreement includes mechanisms for cooperation on regulatory and sustainability issues as well as a dedicated protocol on palm oil to address environmental concerns.

The EU parliament is now expected to greenlight the deal while Indonesian authorities will also complete the ratification process so it can enter into force in 2027.

65 Years of Human Spaceflight at NASA Johnson

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Across those missions, generations of flight controllers, engineers, scientists, instructors, medical specialists, and other experts have helped crews live and work beyond Earth.
  • Sources indicate that when the Manned Spacecraft Center officially opened on Nov.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, for 65 years, NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston has helped shape human spaceflight, from the Gemini missions that demonstrated rendezvous and docking techniques needed for Apollo to the research conducted aboard the International Space Station, which has supported a continuous human presence for more than 26 years. Today, Johnson teams are preparing crews and systems for NASA’s next chapter: returning astronauts to the lunar surface and building the capabilities needed for a long-term human presence at the Moon.

Across those missions, generations of flight controllers, engineers, scientists, instructors, medical specialists, and other experts have helped crews live and work beyond Earth. Johnson is home to NASA’s Orion and Moon Base programs, and its teams continue to support space station operations, astronaut training, spacecraft development, mission operations, and human health.

Sources indicate that when the Manned Spacecraft Center officially opened on Nov. 1, 1961, NASA had already flown two suborbital Mercury missions, with the first orbital flight just months away. Most Project Mercury activities remained at Cape Canaveral in Florida to maintain continuity, but the newly introduced Project Gemini took up residence in Houston, housed in temporary leased facilities across the city while construction of the new Clear Lake campus continued. The new Mission Control Center became NASA’s primary flight control center in June 1965, with the Gemini IV mission that included the first American spacewalk. Houston became the nerve center for American human spaceflight, overseeing the remaining eight Gemini missions before transitioning to the Apollo program. Following the tragic Apollo 1 fire in January 1967, managers, engineers, and astronauts at the Manned Spacecraft Center applied lessons learned to make the spacecraft safer and ensure the safety of its astronauts, resuming crewed missions in October 1968. Managers in Houston devised a daring proposal to send Apollo 8 on a circumlunar flight.

In a recent development, in December 1968, Apollo 8 made its historic trip around the Moon, and seven months later Apollo 11 astronauts Neil Armstrong and Edwin “Buzz” Aldrin landed on the lunar surface. Their first voice transmission back to Earth after their arrival began with the word “Houston.”  Five more Moon landings completed the Apollo program and humanity’s first phase of lunar exploration in December 1972.

Industry observers note that following the Moon landings, scientists at the Manned Spacecraft Center’s Lunar Receiving Laboratory conducted initial analyses of Apollo lunar samples and prepared them for researchers around the world. After the building was demolished in March 2024, the Lunar Receiving Park was dedicated to honor the laboratory’s history in 2026. Today, Johnson’s Astromaterials Research and Exploration Science (ARES) division continues to analyze and curate the Apollo collection at the Lunar Sample Laboratory Facility.

Industry observers note that skylab, America’s first space station, ran into trouble during its launch in May 1973, losing its thermal shield, jamming one solar array and losing the other one. In less than 10 days, engineers in Houston designed and built a sun shield and generated procedures to free the jammed array, followed by the first extensive in-orbit repair activities by the first Skylab crew. The three missions lasting 28, 59, and 84 days accomplished more research than planned, demonstrated the value of humans on long-duration missions, and provided operators in mission control with round-the-clock experience monitoring long duration human spaceflights.

Sources indicate that in July 1975, after several joint training sessions in Houston and Moscow, American astronauts and Soviet cosmonauts met in space for the first time during the Apollo-Soyuz Test Project. Approved as a project in 1972, five approach and landing tests of the space shuttle using orbiter Enterprise paved the way for the first orbital mission of Columbia in 1981.

Sources indicate that engineers in Houston began designs for a reuseable space plane in the late 1960s, with the space shuttle receiving formal approval in 1972. During the 1970s, Johnson Space Center put in place the training and simulation facilities that astronauts used for the life of the program. Upgrades to mission control enabled the use of the latest technologies to support ever more complex space shuttle missions. The April 1981 launch of space shuttle Columbia inaugurated a new era of reusable spacecraft. The program’s 135 missions flew 355 individuals from 16 nations. Missions included satellite deployments and retrievals, dedicated Department of Defense flights, a variety of science missions including deployment of planetary spacecraft, ferrying crews and cargo to two different space stations, and doing the heavy lifting in the assembly of the orbiting laboratory. The program recovered from the tragic losses of the Challenger and Columbia crews with renewed emphasis on crew safety. The final space shuttle mission, STS-135, closed out the 30-year program in July 2011.

Sources indicate that an Earth orbiting space station, first approved by President Ronald Reagan in 1984, underwent many modifications before taking on its current form as the International Space Station in 1993. Overall management of the program resides at Johnson. The first element launch took place in November 1998, followed one month later by the first U.S. element, the Node 1 Unity module. The first expedition crew took up residence on Nov. 2, 2000, and for more than 26 years, rotating crews of astronauts and cosmonauts have lived and worked aboard the orbiting laboratory, establishing a permanent human presence in low Earth orbit.

To date, 298 individuals from 26 countries have visited the space station, conducting more than 4,000 science experiments and educational activities to enable exploration missions and improve life on Earth.

Life aboard the space station depends on a global team on the ground. Crews conduct research and maintain equipment in microgravity, while Johnson teams at the Mission Control Center coordinate the agency’s station operations with international partners. Johnson’s Space Vehicle Mockup Facility supports training for NASA astronauts and international crews on station systems, science operations, and emergency procedures. At the Neutral Buoyancy Laboratory, crews rehearse spacewalks around full-scale station mockups in one of the world’s largest indoor pools. Johnson’s Human Research Program also supports health investigations aboard the station, helping researchers understand how spaceflight affects the body so crews can thrive on future deep space missions.

What began as a framework of modules has evolved into a springboard for international cooperation, advanced scientific research and technology demonstrations, the development of a low Earth orbit economy, and NASA’s next giant leaps in exploration. The space station continues to be a proving ground for NASA’s Artemis program and human exploration of Mars.

Recent findings suggest that the Artemis II mission marked the first crewed flight of NASA’s Orion spacecraft. The four-person crew debuted April 1, on a nearly 10-day trip around the Moon. At its farthest point, Orion traveled 252,756 miles from Earth, farther than any humans had traveled before. The mission demonstrated Orion’s capabilities with astronauts aboard and tested crew operations in deep space, setting the stage for future lunar missions.

Building on Artemis II, NASA’s Artemis III mission will test integrated operations in low Earth orbit between Orion and test versions of one or both commercial human landing systems under development by SpaceX and Blue Origin. Astronauts will demonstrate the rendezvous and docking capabilities needed to transfer crews between spacecraft for the lunar landing planned for Artemis IV.

NASA’s Moon Base Program is planning a phased effort to support a sustained human presence near the Moon’s South Pole. The first phase will focus on robotic exploration, technology demonstrations, and preparations for future surface operations. Later phases will add infrastructure to support astronauts living and working on the Moon. Lunar terrain vehicles will help crews explore farther, transport equipment, and conduct science.

It has been revealed that at Johnson, teams are drawing on decades of experience in astronaut training, mission control, spacecraft development, and human health to prepare for these missions. From training crews for lunar operations to developing the systems that will support them, Johnson is building on 65 years of human spaceflight experience for humanity’s return to the lunar surface through the Artemis and Moon Base Programs.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Industry observers note that the research, published in Nature Communications, challenges the conventional explanation for the origins of cellular structures known as encapsulins.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, researchers at the University of Miami have discovered a previously unknown group of viruses that could help explain a missing piece of evolutionary history. The finding reveals an unexpected connection between viruses and tiny protein compartments inside cells, offering new clues about how some of life's earliest biological structures may have developed.

Industry observers note that the research, published in Nature Communications, challenges the conventional explanation for the origins of cellular structures known as encapsulins. Scientists previously believed these compartments evolved from viruses. However, the newly introduced evidence suggests a more complicated evolutionary relationship in which viruses and encapsulins may have repeatedly evolved from one another over millions of years.

The discovery could have crucial implications for biotechnology and for understanding the origins and early evolution of life. It also raises the possibility that viruses have biological functions that scientists have largely overlooked.

Mysterious New Viruses Reveal an Evolutionary Connection.

At the center of the discovery are proteins that fold into a distinctive three-dimensional structure known as the HK97-fold. These proteins can assemble into protective shells and are found in both viruses and encapsulins.

The newly identified viruses have smaller, simpler genomes than other viruses that produce HK97-fold protein shells. They also possess characteristics associated with both viruses and encapsulins, making them possible evolutionary intermediates between the two. Studying these unusual viruses could help researchers understand how increasingly complex biological systems first appeared.

"What makes the HK97-fold proteins so interesting is that they can form shells that enclose biochemical reactions in cellular lineages, archaea, and bacteria. But they also serve genetic purposes in viruses, storing and protecting their viral genome," remarked Abelardo Aguilar, the study's first author and a Ph.D. student in the Department of Biology at the University of Miami College of Arts and Sciences.

"These proteins build compartments with two different roles, which connects directly with the study of the origin of life and its early evolution because if you think about it, life at its core is about enclosing reactions and also enclosing information that can be inherited so those reactions can happen in the future.".

AI Helps Discover Hidden Viruses in Billions of DNA Sequences.

To uncover these previously unknown viruses, Aguilar worked with Antoni Luque Santolaria, the study's senior author and an associate professor in the Department of Biology. Luque also holds secondary appointments in the Department of Physics within the College of Arts and Sciences and the Department of Chemical, Environmental and Materials Engineering in the College of Engineering. The project brought together collaborators from multiple institutions.

Rather than relying on laboratory experiments to grow viruses, the team searched enormous genetic databases containing billions of DNA sequences. They combined bioinformatics, models of protein behavior, and artificial intelligence tools, including protein language models and AlphaFold, to investigate the structures encoded by these sequences.

The databases included IMG/M, a resource associated with the U.S. Department of Energy's Joint Genome Institute and the University of California, Berkeley. Its genetic information comes from environmental samples collected around the world, including soil, seawater, wastewater, the human gut, and numerous other locations.

This approach allows scientists to investigate viruses that have never been successfully grown in a laboratory, greatly expanding the number of organisms and evolutionary relationships they can study.

"The majority of viruses cannot be grown in the lab. But now through sequencing, we have access to information on viruses for which we don't know the host, that we can't culture in the lab, but that are everywhere," Luque explained. "That means there are multiple questions in relation to evolution and how viruses have adapted to the world that it's now possible to explore bioinformatically.".

Viral Protein Shells May Have Unexpected Functions.

Beyond identifying the upcoming viruses, the researchers proposed a possible molecular explanation for how viruses and encapsulins could have evolved from one another.

Their model centers on procapsids, immature viral protein shells (capsids) that may provide a pathway between the two types of structures. These shells could potentially support both genetic functions, such as containing viral DNA, and metabolic functions involving chemical reactions.

This raises an intriguing possibility. Viral capsids are generally recognized for packaging and protecting genetic material, but certain forms might also help create environments where biochemical reactions can occur.

"One implication of this research is the possibility that viral capsids could also facilitate biochemical reactions, which would open up the potential roles that capsids have in environments as a whole," Aguilar explained.

Although further research is needed to establish these potential functions, the findings suggest that scientists may need to look beyond the infectious stages of viruses to fully understand their roles in nature.

"When we're looking at viruses, we tend to look only at the particles that are infective, and this study points out that we might need to start putting more emphasis on the non-infective versions of the virus and what other functions those viral-like particles may have that we have overlooked in the past.".

New AI Tools Open the Door to More Viral Discoveries.

The research also demonstrates how artificial intelligence and computational biology are transforming the study of viruses. By combining powerful analytical tools with knowledge of protein structure and physical behavior, scientists can now investigate evolutionary questions that were previously difficult to explore.

Industry observers note that supported by the Gordon and Betty Moore Foundation and the U.S. National Science Foundation, the project provides a framework for studying other poorly understood viruses and their biological capabilities.

The researchers believe these methods could also be useful beyond evolutionary biology, including efforts to understand newly emerging viruses and pathogens.

"If you have the right question and you pair it with the right tools and physical insights, it gives researchers an opportunity to look at viruses in a way that we didn't have an opportunity to do before," Luque noted. "There are evolution questions, but there are also questions about emerging pathogens or emerging viruses. The set of tools that we use can be moved forward in different contexts.".

"[It's] a healthy sign that guests are responding to our changes and choosing Target more often," CEO Michael Fiddelke told reporters.

Digital comparable sales jumped nearly 10% during the quarter.

Recent findings suggest that encouraged by the growth, Target raised its full-year guidance, upping its net sales growth guidance by 1 percentage point to around 6%. The company also mentioned it's now projecting full-year earnings per share to be in a range of $10.65 to $11.40, compared with prior guidance of between $9.90 and $10.90.

"The changes we've made across our assortment and guest experience are adding up," Fiddelke told reporters. "While we're encouraged by the progress, we know there's more work ahead to sustain this momentum and deliver consistent growth over time.".

Target shares climbed about 7% in afternoon trading Wednesday.

Here's how the company performed in its fiscal third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:.

Sources indicate that for the quarter ended Oct. 31, Target reported net income of $1.21 billion, or $2.65 per share, up from $689 million, or $1.51 per share, a year earlier.

It has been revealed that this year, the company said it's invested approximately $3.8 billion in capital expenditures, up nearly $1 billion from last year. Because of those returns, Fiddelke said Target is now expecting to invest between $5 billion and $6 billion in capex next year.

On a call with analysts, he added that those investments will go toward more store remodels, technology, supply chain improvements, among other initiatives.

Sources indicate that the company stated it saw particular strength in beauty, which saw 9% growth, and food and beverage, where sales increased nearly 7%. The retailer added that net sales rose in all three months of the third quarter, with the strongest performance during the back-to-school season.

Fiddelke told reporters the quarter's strength showed "continued progress" toward Target's priorities that it outlined at the beginning of its turnaround.

Fiddelke said Target is "encouraged" by shopping behaviors it's seen so far in the current quarter.

In a recent development, it's also lowered prices on more than 10,000 items in an effort to get customers back into its stores, especially as consumer sentiment lags and inflation remains high. Target's stock is up more than 70% this year.

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (458 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Space

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers have spotted an ancient, "dead" Martian volcano from orbit around the Red Planet.
  • The European Space Agency's Mars Express spacecraft, which has been orbiting and studying the planet since it arrived in 2003, recently captured incredible new imagery of the volcano Tharsis Tholus.
  • This snapshot was captured by the spacecraft's High Resolution Stereo Camera.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers have spotted an ancient, "dead" Martian volcano from orbit around the Red Planet.

The European Space Agency's Mars Express spacecraft, which has been orbiting and studying the planet since it arrived in 2003, recently captured incredible new imagery of the volcano Tharsis Tholus.

This snapshot was captured by the spacecraft's High Resolution Stereo Camera.

Even as old and worn as it is, the Martian volcano stands at around 4.97 miles (8 kilometers) tall which is comparable to some of the highest peaks in the Himalayan mountains.

Despite its impressive height, it's still only about a medium-sized volcano for Mars, which is home much more impressively-sized volcanoes. For example, the planet's largest volcano Olympus Mons measures in at roughly 13.2 miles high (21.3 kilometers).

While Tharsis Tholus might not be the tallest volcano on Mars, it is incredibly steep. It is steeper than Mauna Kea in Hawaii on Earth. To fully showcase the volcano's structure and topography in 3D, researchers actually exaggerated the vertical scale in this image, ESA reported.

Sources indicate that in addition to being steep and fairly tall, the volcano also has an interesting history. You can see that it is speckled with what look like small holes which are actually craters created by impacts from objects like asteroids. The volcano's current, unique shape is a combined effort by these impacts, environmental factors causing erosion and warping and ancient lava flows that left behind built-up material.

Industry observers note that the observations by Mars Express also reveals cracks and other imperfections in the volcano. All of these details might seem like superficial bits of detail, however every small crater, every lumpy cliffside and every worn down surface hides information about the planet's past.

By studying features like volcanoes on Mars, researchers can piece together what the planet may have looked like in its ancient past. How active was this volcano? How did it interact with the landscape around it? Observations like this can hold the answers.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The current flagship television from Sony, the Bravia 9 II, is an RGB TV model (Sony calls it “True RGB”) that brings to life even the darkest scenes in Game of Thrones. Much brighter than the midrange Bravia 7 II, the 9 II's best qualities are related to its black levels, picture quality, and excellent viewing angles that allow me to see Jon Snow and the GoT dragons perfectly, even when I'm sitting off to the side.

This premium Sony television carries a premium price of $3,600 for the 65-inch model, but that’s still $1,400 less than the LG Micro RGB Evo, which retails for $5,000. I ended up preferring the overall picture quality of that LG model and some other OLED models, but—after my usual rigorous testing—I felt the Bravia 9 II came close to matching the high caliber of those other options. In fact, it’s just a notch or two lower than the absolute best television you might find.

In a recent development, the Sony Bravia 9 II is all black, sits on two feet, and includes four HDMI ports (only two are HDMI 2.1, though, which allows for higher-bandwidth streaming and sound at 48 Gbps). Setup was a breeze; Google TV was up and running in less than five minutes, which is an impressive feat, given that both Samsung and LG televisions typically add a few extra steps to the install process, such as authenticating your login (with Samsung) or relying on an app (with the LG ThinQ).

Industry observers note that the premium Sony Bravia 9 II also offers exceptional sound. It includes two upfiring tweeters for more realistic Dolby Atmos than the Bravia 7 II, which lacks these extra channels. When I watched House of the Dragon, the room-filling audio made me feel like I was flying a dragon or piloting a ship.

According to recent reports, viewing angles on the Bravia 9 II are about the best I’ve seen on any television. I tested this element by camping out in a chair and playing video games off to the side, and there wasn’t a hint of screen glare. These perks are, again, a sign of its premium quality, verified through my usual benchmarks. Skin tones looked varied and vivid; one person had a little more red in her face than what I noticed on the LG Micro RGB Evo or the Samsung Micro RGB R95H.

It has been revealed that in a demo-reel benchmark test I use for all televisions, I was shocked by the Bravia 9 II's stellar performance. I’ve watched the same short segment with a fence in front of a winter landscape countless times to test various models, but here, the green grass in the background looked supremely vivid and clear. It’s because the Bravia 9 II has such exceptional screen brightness, color accuracy, and absolutely no glare.

According to recent reports, the Sony remote is just OK. I wish the Home button were centered; since it's not, I kept clicking the mic for the Google Gemini voicebot (which is in the center) by mistake. I prefer the bare-bones Samsung remote or the one included with an Apple TV 4K streaming device. Just give me a Netflix button and volume controls, and I’m good. Still, the layout of this remote mostly makes sense, and I like that it’s backlit.

The Bravia 9 II didn’t pass all of my tests for performance while I watched indicates and movies, but it did allow me to tweak more settings than I’m used to. For example, the TV automatically calibrated colors and tones for Spider-Man: Brand Fresh Day, but it still looked too dark. I was able to manually adjust the black level and used Vivid mode to make Spidey’s suit look extra red.

Sources indicate that however, compared to the picture quality of an OLED like the Samsung S95H, the Bravia 9 II's deep blacks looked less realistic. That's because on OLED TVs, the LEDs can be turned off entirely. The Bravia 9 II performed OK for Toy Story 5, but in darker scenes late in the film, I noticed the Samsung had inky blacks that reminded me of a high-end projector.

My main takeaway is that it's nice that you can tweak settings on the Bravia 9 II to great effect, thanks to an RGB panel that’s super-bright. The movies Awake and The Creator tested my patience a little in that regard. I adjusted the black level to precisely 61 (out of 100) and could then see faces, a predawn mountain scene, and a beach landing with better clarity. Knowing you can achieve those results is nice; actually doing it does take time.

Industry observers note that while playing Resident Evil: Requiem to test brightness, picture quality, and latency, I confirmed that it's possible to adjust the black level to liven up dark scenes. I also noticed that the latency, at a 120-Hz refresh rate when I used one of the HDMI 2.1 ports, was almost nonexistent. That helped with every slight twitch when a seven-headed monster from the dark underworld of hell started attacking me.

It has been revealed that similar games, like Senua's Saga: Hellblade II, looked too gray and washed out on the midrange Bravia 7 II and some LED models I’ve tested. I also played End of Abyss, a game that takes place almost entirely in dark hallways, and the Bravia 9 II rendered those scenes with inky blacks—granted, not as black as an OLED would, but better than many LED TVs.

Recent findings suggest that bravia 9 II lived up to its flagship-quality promise for sportscasts, making my beloved Minnesota Vikings' purple jerseys look vivid and clear and the grass bright green—all without displaying any glare at all. News programs were bright, with strong color accuracy, but not oversaturated—a good compromise. In fact, it was so clear, I felt as if I could reach out to clip an MS Now analyst's nose hairs.

It has been revealed that the Bravia 9 II is near the top of the leaderboard of the best televisions to buy right now. You'll just want to consider the technology it uses. RGB models use red, green, and blue LEDs to create realistic colors that, in theory, improve color accuracy and vividness. Unlike an OLED TV, an RGB TV still shines those LED colors through an LCD panel. So you have to pick your poison. The Bravia 9 II looked super bright and vivid, especially during NFL games. It’s just a hair less colorful and vivid compared to the LG Micro RGB Evo.

Industry observers note that knowing you can tweak the settings for the results you want and that anyone in your household will be able to see America’s Got Talent from any angle in the room is a major plus. But is the Sony Bravia 9 II worth $3,600 when so many TVs cost around $2,000? I would say it depends on what you watch. I want to see dragons at night and monsters in dark hallways, but for some animated shows, sports, and network TV, you might just want your device to work well, right out of the box, without worrying about cinematic quality. Yes, a flagship lets you do a lot more, but at a much steeper price.

#139061. Breaking: Laser Focus at the Top of the World

Breaking: Laser Focus at the Top of the World

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (803 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nasa

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A next-generation geodetic instrument developed by NASA, part of a network that helps measure satellites’ orbits and the planet’s shape, has debuted in Svalbard, Norway.
  • More than 60 years ago, scientists at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center aimed a laser skyward and fired a pulse of light at an orbiting satellite equipped with special reflectors.
  • It has been revealed that since then, satellite laser ranging (SLR) has grown more precise and more widely used.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A next-generation geodetic instrument developed by NASA, part of a network that helps measure satellites’ orbits and the planet’s shape, has debuted in Svalbard, Norway.

More than 60 years ago, scientists at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center aimed a laser skyward and fired a pulse of light at an orbiting satellite equipped with special reflectors. By measuring the time it took for the light to return, they demonstrated a fresh, more precise method for tracking satellites.

It has been revealed that since then, satellite laser ranging (SLR) has grown more precise and more widely used. The technique now underpins many aspects of Earth observation, such as validating satellite orbits and mapping subtle changes to Earth’s surface. Pioneered at the Goddard Optical Research Facility—now the Goddard Geophysical and Astronomical Observatory—laser ranging is performed at more than 40 stations worldwide.

In 2026, the next generation of SLR, developed by NASA scientists and tested at Goddard, began to come online. On October 12, a faster, even more precise SLR system officially debuted at the Ny-Ålesund Geodetic Observatory in Svalbard, Norway, operated by the Norwegian Mapping Authority, a NASA partner. The observatory’s remote location in the Arctic archipelago is shown in this image, acquired with the OLI (Operational Land Imager) on Landsat 9 in July 2026. It is the first NASA next-generation SLR system in operation and the northernmost SLR facility on Earth.

While the systems developed decades ago have been “workhorses” of the global laser tracking network, their age and the growing number of satellites have necessitated updates, said Stephen Merkowitz, project manager for NASA’s Space Geodesy Project. “We wanted newer systems that could track more objects, and track them more accurately and precisely,” he said.

In a recent development, years of development, testing, and careful calibration produced the Space Geodesy Satellite Laser Ranging system now running at Ny-Ålesund. Among its features are lasers that can fire pulses thousands of times per second, up from tens of times per second, and sensors that can detect single photons, meaning that less light needs to be reflected back from a satellite.

According to recent reports, along with determining the orbits of satellites, SLR is critical for establishing the terrestrial reference frame, the foundation of modern coordinate systems and a common standard that allows measurements to be compared with one another. “If you want to know where your satellite observation is on a map, you need to have it in the proper reference frame,” Merkowitz said. In addition, tracking Earth’s center of mass, measuring changes in sea level and ice mass, studying the motion of tectonic plates, and maintaining global navigation satellite systems such as GPS, all rely on an accurate reference frame.

The far-north location of the Ny-Ålesund facility improves the distribution of SLR stations across the planet, making the whole network more robust. The location also allows the system to gather more data about polar-orbiting satellites, which include ICESat-2, GRACE-FO, and other Earth observation satellites. “From the station at Goddard [in Greenbelt, Maryland], we’ll catch the polar-orbiting satellites maybe two or three times a day,” Merkowitz said. “But from Ny-Ålesund, you’ll see them almost every orbit.”.

Certain satellite missions may especially benefit from the Arctic location, he added. Take ICESat-2, designed to make precise observations of ice surface heights. Having a station tracking the satellite from an icy polar region could lead to more accurate measurements there. “When it’s over the ice, we want the calibration to be as good as possible,” Merkowitz mentioned.

Sources indicate that innovations and lessons learned from the Svalbard installation will carry over to future ones, Merkowitz noted. In particular, the Ny-Ålesund facility drove improvements in automation because the site is located next to a bird sanctuary. Access restrictions require the station to be remotely operated at certain times, such as during the summer breeding season for migratory birds. These capabilities can be refined and applied at other stations. NASA is currently building two more next-generation SLR systems to replace legacy instruments at Goddard and the McDonald Geodetic Observatory in Texas.

Archaeologists reveal a powerful Iron Age king may have been a woman

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1101 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that new archaeological research from Bournemouth University (BU) suggests that an influential Iron Age British ruler, long believed to have been a man, was actually a woman.
  • Verica ruled the Atrebates, a powerful tribe whose lands extended across much of what is now Hampshire and West Sussex.
  • The Roman historian Cassius Dio claimed that Verica's appeal was the reason Claudius decided to invade Britain.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that new archaeological research from Bournemouth University (BU) suggests that an influential Iron Age British ruler, long believed to have been a man, was actually a woman. The ruler, known as Verica, played a pivotal role in events leading to the Roman invasion of Britain in AD 43. The findings challenge longstanding assumptions about early British history and the political influence of women during this period.

Verica ruled the Atrebates, a powerful tribe whose lands extended across much of what is now Hampshire and West Sussex. Around AD 40, Verica was forced from power and escaped to Rome, where the exiled ruler sought assistance from Emperor Claudius.

The Roman historian Cassius Dio claimed that Verica's appeal was the reason Claudius decided to invade Britain. If this account is accurate, Verica's actions may have helped set in motion one of the most consequential events in British history.

Ancient Evidence Challenges an Iron Age King's Identity.

Dr. Miles Russell, Director of Archaeological Fieldwork at Bournemouth University, led the research and argues that earlier historians incorrectly identified Verica as male.

"Verica is assumed to have been male because of the patriarchal mindset of 19th-century classical historians. Verica was not only critical to the special relationship between Britain and Rome in the early first century AD but was indisputably female.".

In a recent development, russell points to several pieces of evidence supporting this interpretation. One is the name Verica itself, which ends in the letter "a," a feature common among female names of the time. Other prominent examples include Cartimandua, who ruled the Brigantes (in Yorkshire), and Boudica, leader of the Iceni (in Norfolk).

All three rulers lived during roughly the same period. Boudica is the best known because of her rebellion against Roman rule in AD 60. However, Russell argues that Verica may have held even greater political power and influence.

Recent findings suggest that another crucial clue comes from coins issued under Verica's rule. These coins bear the Latin title "rex," traditionally translated as "king," which has contributed to the assumption that Verica was male. Russell explains that the title was not necessarily restricted to men.

"People also assume she was a 'he' because of the term 'rex' on coins, but rex is a non-gender-specific title; both male and female kings were recognized by Rome, Cleopatra of Egypt being the most famous.".

He continued: "The use of the Latin title rex on coins indicates that Verica ruled with the full authorization of the emperor.".

The artwork on Verica's coins provides another intriguing clue. Rather than depicting the masculine warriors commonly featured on coins produced by other British Iron Age rulers, Verica's coins show a figure with distinctly feminine characteristics.

"Whilst other coin-producing British Iron Age leaders portray obviously male warriors, Verica is depicted as a slender, feminine, bare-breasted figure riding on horseback.".

The Forgotten Ruler Behind Rome's Invasion of Britain.

Russell believes Verica's importance extended far beyond the ruler's identity. He argues that Verica may have been instrumental in helping Claudius successfully invade Britain.

Sources indicate that ancient Roman writers frequently portrayed Claudius as an ineffective emperor who was easily influenced by women and formerly enslaved people who had gained their freedom. This reputation may have shaped how historians described Verica's role in persuading him to invade.

Russell suggests that Cassius Dio's account reinforced this negative portrayal by presenting the invasion as a decision made under the influence of a woman. In reality, he argues, Verica may have been a valuable political and military ally who supplied the Romans with intelligence and practical assistance.

It has been revealed that "The story of Claudius committing to something only because a woman told him to fits the trope of this emperor as being submissive and henpecked. In effect, Dio was saying that the campaign was undertaken solely because of the whisperings of a barbarian femme fatale. Verica's role was rather more central to the British expedition. Having her on board ensured the project was a success, as she provided tactical information and support on the ground.

"The invasion was Claudius' great triumph -- it being the only chance he had to prove he was a successful military leader. Verica provided the excuse for regime change, and the emperor seized it.".

Industry observers note that for Claudius, the conquest of Britain offered an opportunity to establish his reputation as a successful military commander. Verica's removal from power gave him a political justification for intervening, while the exiled ruler's knowledge of Britain may have helped the Roman forces achieve their objectives.

Could Rome's Conquest of Britain Have Been Avoided?

Although Verica was an notable political figure in late Iron Age Britain, the ruler's influence has received relatively little attention compared with that of other prominent leaders.

In a recent development, russell believes the archaeological evidence supports recognizing Verica as one of Britain's earliest and most significant female rulers. He also raises the possibility that the Roman invasion might never have occurred without Verica's exile and subsequent appeal to Claudius.

According to recent reports, "We should take the archaeological evidence at face value" notes Russell "and remember Verica as a female-king and one of the earliest and most important of British female leaders. Had she not been deposed, fleeing to Claudius for military support, Rome may never have invaded Britain in the first place.".

New Insights Into Women in Iron Age Britain.

The findings build on earlier Bournemouth University research exploring the position of women in ancient British society.

Last year, a study involving Russell and other BU researchers uncovered evidence of a matriarchal society in Iron Age Britain. The research indicated that husbands moved into their wives' communities after marriage, suggesting that women occupied a central position in the social structure.

Together, these discoveries are prompting researchers to reconsider the influence women may have exercised in Iron Age Britain, both within their communities and in the political decisions that shaped the region's future.

It has been revealed that russell's research on Verica is presented in the latest book Caratacus: Great king of Britain, published by Bloomsbury in January (ISBN 9781350477902). The findings are also discussed in the latest edition of Current Archaeology.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A Russian helicopter is suspected of violating Finnish airspace, the Nordic country's Ministry of Defense said Saturday.

The incident happened a few hours after a drone attack left a Russian cargo ship ablaze in the Gulf of Finland, the easternmost part of the Baltic Sea.

In a recent development, according to Finland's Defense Ministry, the incursion happened at 12:34 p.m. local time (10:34 UTC/GMT) off the town of Loviisa, on the southern coast.

"This alleged airspace violation may be linked to rescue or surveillance operations carried out by Finland following damage sustained by a cargo ship in the Gulf of Finland," public broadcaster YLE cited Defense Minister Antti Hakkanen as saying.

The ministry added the helicopter could have penetrated up to 4.1 kilometers (2.5 miles) into Finnish territory.

Earlier Saturday, Finland — one of NATO's newest members — stated a Russian cargo ship heading for Russia's Baltic exclave of Kaliningrad caught fire after being struck by drones in the Gulf of Finland.

The Finnish military said the Sparta II was damaged ⁠west ⁠of Russia's Gogland island, about 40 kilometers (25 miles) from Finland's coast, and later drifted into Finnish territorial waters.

Finnish ‌Border ​Guard Commander Ilja Iljin later told YLE that the vessel, which is known to have links to the Russian military, was struck by Ukrainian  drones while in Russian waters.

"At the moment, ​there is no confirmed information ⁠about ​what cargo ​is on board, ​but it ‌cannot be ruled out ​that ⁠there is military materiel on ⁠board," ​Iljin said.

The ship is on a US sanctions list, according to a search of the Open Sanctions website.

The Border Guard later stated the crew of the Sparta II was evacuating into a life raft and rescue boat.

"The [Ukraine] war is spilling over into our neighbouring areas," wrote Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo on X.

Ukraine has the right to fight against the aggressor," he added.

The Finnish government has put temporary curbs on aviation and maritime traffic in the eastern Gulf of Finland.

The Defense Ministry said Finland had informed its allies about the incident.

What OPEC's surprise oil cut means for gas prices

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • OPEC and its allies’ surprise move to slash oil production will soon be felt at US gas pumps.
  • In a recent development, the group known as OPEC+ declared Sunday it would cut oil production by more than 1.6 million barrels a day starting in May, running through the end of the year.
  • Sources indicate that the production cut announcement also had an immediate impact on gasoline futures, which will be passed onto US drivers much more quickly than the spike in oil prices.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

OPEC and its allies’ surprise move to slash oil production will soon be felt at US gas pumps.

In a recent development, the group known as OPEC+ declared Sunday it would cut oil production by more than 1.6 million barrels a day starting in May, running through the end of the year. The news sent both Brent crude futures, the global oil benchmark, and WTI, the US benchmark, up about 6% in trading Monday.

Sources indicate that the production cut announcement also had an immediate impact on gasoline futures, which will be passed onto US drivers much more quickly than the spike in oil prices. RBOB, the most closely watched wholesale gasoline price, was up about 8 cents a gallon, or about 3%, in morning trading.

Recent findings suggest that “I think OPEC is reawakening the inflation monster,” stated Tom Kloza, global head of energy analysis for OPIS, which tracks gas prices for AAA. “The White House has to be shocked and major-time pissed. It certainly alters the calculus for a while.”.

The national average for US gas prices stood at $3.51, on Monday, according to AAA. Kloza stated he could see it getting up to $3.80 to $3.90 in relatively short order thanks to the move by OPEC.

“We’re not going to get back to $5 a gallon. I don’t think we’re even going as high as $4,” he noted. But he said by the end of the summer US drivers could be back above year-earlier prices, especially if there is a hurricane or other storms affecting production along the Gulf Coast.

The average US regular gas price a year ago stood at $4.19 a gallon in the wake of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and the disruption that caused to world’s energy markets. Prices eventually reached a record $5.02 a gallon on June 14, before starting a slow but steady decline over the course of more than three months during which the average price fell every day. The decline was partly driven by the release of oil from the US Strategic Petroleum Reserve, and partly by concerns that there could be a US or global recession that reduced the demand for gasoline.

Oil prices surge after OPEC+ producers announce surprise cuts.

According to recent reports, even at $3.51, US gas prices were just below the $3.53 average on Feb. 23, 2022, the day before Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

Industry observers note that kloza mentioned one thing keeping prices from getting anywhere near the record levels of 2022 is that the US aims additional releases from the SPR, and US oil production and refining capacity are both up. But a cut of 1 million barrels a day of oil by OPEC+ will not be easy to make up.

“They have ability to cut production and they seem motivated to do so,” he mentioned.
